On this day chapter 37 of the Gaiad is read, telling the story of ## The Great Circulatory Innovation ### The Problem and Solution - **Chordatus** (son of Dutrus) and **Annelidus** faced a serious issue - Both supported by **hydrostatic pressure** (water pressure in body cavity) - **Problem**: Movement disrupted circulation, organs couldn't stay nourished - **Solution**: Built hearts with **closed circulatory systems** (arteries and veins) - This marked evolution from **hydrostatic to circulatory** systems ## Annelon's Lineage - The Great Worm Radiation ### Annelon → Two Primary Lines - **Segmentus** - the segmented body plan line - **Ribbon** - the hunting specialists #### Ribbon's Line → Ribbon Worms (Nemerteans) - Built a **long, venomous proboscis** for hunting - Modern **Ribbon Worms** use "poison darts shot straight into the heart" - Specialized predatory lifestyle #### Segmentus → The Great Segmented Worm Families ##### Segmentus → Pleistos and Amphon ###### Amphon's Children - **Amphinos** → **fire worms** with poison spikes and bright warning colors - Modern flags show "colors that bestow great honor to Amphinos' line" - **Sipuncula** → became her own phylum (**peanut worms**) ###### Pleistos → Vermo and Errantius ####### Errantius → Free-Swimming Predatory Worms - **Myzo** - the parasite - **Greatswimmer** → **Phyllos** and **Eunice** **Eunice's Story**: Jealous and violent, "stole her husband's manhood" and conceived daughters alone - Her daughters = **Bobbit Worms** (fierce predatory marine worms) **Phyllos → Diverse Swimming Forms**: - **Syllides** - lazy reproduction by budding body parts monthly - **Tomopteris** - breaks fins "as chaff," permanent swimmer - **Alciops** - "hawkeyed hunter" with exceptional eyesight - **Aphrodite** - "ancestress of sea mice," beautiful daughters ####### Vermo → The Terrestrial and Specialized Lines **Vermo's Four Daughters**: - **Eartha** - the great wanderer - **Sapion** - the wise one - **Hestia** - the deep-sea specialist - **Orbinida** - of eternal fame **Sapion → Sabella and Spiona**: - **Sabella** → **feather duster worms** - "fishermen" that beautify temples - **Spiona** → tentacled forms **Hestia → Deep-Sea Chemosynthetic Worms**: - Closed her gut, uses bacteria for energy - **Riftia** → hydrothermal vent worms - **Lamella** → cold seep worms (oil-rich environments) **Eartha → Terraclithia and Echiuron**: - **Echiuron** → became own phylum due to unique creativity - **Terraclithia** → **Terebella** and **Clitella** **Terebella's Three Sons**: - **Spaghettes** - uses tentacles "like ropes" to catch distant prey - **Pompeii** - lives in volcanic environments - **Acros** → **Squidworm** and **Swima** (deep-sea swimmers) **Clitella → The Terrestrial Success**: - Small head but great wisdom, prolific offspring - Children took to rivers and land - **Earthworms** - soil tillers - **Leeches** - blood feeders ("both bitter and sweet") ## Key Evolutionary Innovations ### Circulatory System - **Closed circulation** with hearts, arteries, and veins - Solved the problem of organ nourishment during movement - Foundation for all complex bilateral animals ### Segmentation - **Segmentus** built body with countless segments - Each segment with its own pair of legs and bristles - Provided resilience and redundancy ### Specialized Hunting - **Ribbon worms**: Venomous proboscis - **Bobbit worms**: Ambush predation - **Various polychaetes**: Different feeding strategies ### Habitat Specialization - **Deep-sea vents**: Riftia (chemosynthetic) - **Cold seeps**: Lamella (oil environments) - **Volcanic areas**: Pompeii worms - **Terrestrial**: Earthworms and leeches - **Parasitic**: Myzo and leech lines ### Reproductive Strategies - **Syllides**: Epitoky (reproductive budding) - **Eunice**: Parthenogenesis (asexual reproduction) - **Clitella**: High fecundity ## Biological Connections - **Nemerteans** (ribbon worms) - real proboscis predators - **Polychaetes** - diverse marine segmented worms - **Sipunculans** - peanut worms (now considered part of Annelida) - **Echiurans** - spoon worms (now considered annelids) - **Oligochaetes** - earthworms and freshwater worms - **Hirudineans** - leeches - **Riftia pachyptila** - giant tube worms at hydrothermal vents - **Bobbit worms** (Eunice aphroditois) - ambush predators - **Sabellids** - feather duster worms (filter feeders) ## Major Themes - **Circulatory revolution**: From hydrostatic to closed circulatory systems - **Segmentation advantage**: Redundancy and specialization - **Habitat diversification**: From marine to terrestrial, from surface to deep-sea vents - **Reproductive innovations**: Various strategies for different environments - **Beauty and function**: Even predatory worms (fire worms, feather dusters) can be beautiful - **Ecosystem roles**: From soil tillers to deep-sea chemosynthetic farmers The chapter establishes annelid worms as key innovators in both circulatory physiology and ecological diversification, with modern representatives in almost every aquatic and terrestrial habitat.

"poor and weak, had no strength to seek great things" - Built only "small and brainless state - a kingdom with no fate" ### Molluscus - The Great Success - Bore **many sons**, "more than any other patriarch could claim" - On this day chapter 40 of the Gaiad is read, telling the story of Chapter notes: # Chapter 40: The First Extinction and Mollusk Rise - Detailed Notes **Source:** Old Gaiad Chapter 31 **New Chapter:** 40 **Era:** End-Botomian Extinction Event (Early Cambrian) **Title:** "The First Extinction and Mollusk Rise" ## Major Theme: Survival Through Building and Innovation ### The First Mass Extinction Event - **Fire from Sky**: Meteorite impact or volcanic catastrophe - **Divine Battle**: Hengweh vs Mithra wrestling in heaven - **Blocked Sun**: Ash/debris blocking solar radiation - **Mass Mortality**: Many lineages went extinct - **Historical Marker**: End of Botomian Stage (Early Cambrian) ### Victims of Extinction - **Archaeocyathids**: Completely extinct (reef-builders) - **Trilobites**: Barely survived (major decline) - **Brachiopods**: Barely survived (reduced diversity) - **Hyoliths**: Barely survived (cone-shaped animals) ### Divine Selection of Survivors - **Wiwaxius Chosen**: Selected by Mithra to restore life - **Mission**: "Restore life to the world, protect from future extinctions" - **Evolutionary Role**: Ancestor of mollusks chosen for survival traits ## Mollusk Radiation (From Wiwaxius) ### Wiwaxius' Two Sons - **Molluscus**: Successful builder, founded diverse mollusk phylum - **Kamptos**: Poor builder, created small brainless kingdom (possibly Kamptozoa) ### Molluscus' Innovation Strategy - **Many Sons**: Diversification approach - **Building Focus**: Emphasis on shell construction - **Eldest Son**: Testar the sixteen-plated (most successful) ## Shell Architecture Evolution ### Testar's Innovation - **Sixteen-Plated Shell**: Complex multi-valve design - **Organization**: Eight valves right, eight valves left - **Thick Construction**: Strong protective structure - **Architectural Precision**: Organized, systematic building ### Brothers' Failures - **Solenos**: Became parasitic blood-drinker (targeting cnidarians) - **Caudos**: Became predator of foraminifera - **Work Ethic**: Neither invested in shell-building - **Evolutionary Dead Ends**: Poor building led to limited success ## Major Mollusk Lineages ### First Split: Chiton vs Conchifer - **Chiton Horizontus**: Horizontal shell unification - **Conchifer Verticus**: Vertical shell unification - **Architectural Divergence**: Two different approaches to shell organization ### Chiton Lineage → Polyplacophora - **Eight Shells in Row**: Horizontal arrangement - **Rolling Defense**: Roll up when threatened - **Brain Reduction**: Traded intelligence for simple armor - **Modern Legacy**: Chitons still have eight-plated shells ### Conchifer Lineage → Bivalvia & Others - **Vertical Unification**: Left shell + right shell - **Two Sons**: Bivos (hinged) and Monos (unified) #### Bivos → Bivalves - **Hinged Shell Design**: Two shells connected by hinge - **Sand Dwelling**: Lived buried in sediment - **Filter Feeding**: Fished food from water - **Defensive Closure**: Closed shells when threatened - **Convergent Evolution**: Looked like brachiopods (Brachios line) - **Modern Examples**: Clams, mussels, oysters #### Monos → Monoplacophorans - **Single Shell**: Merged two shells into one - **Initial Struggles**: Limited early success - **Identity Crisis**: "Nothing but single shell as identity" - **Living Fossils**: Small group surviving today ### Carlos the Curly's Innovation - **Exploration**: Walked across seas discovering new habitats - **Grandson of Monos**: Third generation breakthrough - **Two Sons**: Gastropus and Digitos #### Gastropus → Gastropods - **Spiral Innovation**: Twisted body and shell into spiral - **Strength Through Coiling**: Each generation curled more - **Shell Strength**: Spiral provided superior protection - **Snail Ancestry**: All snails descended from spiral innovation - **Diversification**: From tiny garden snails to giant conchs #### Digitos' Innovation - **Foot Modification**: Converted foot into tentacles - **Two Sons**: Cephalopus and Scaphopus ##### Cephalopus → Cephalopods - **Intelligence**: Studied hard, developed large brain - **Buoyancy Innovation**: Learned to fly using gas-filled chambers - **Coiling Shell**: Built spiral shell with flotation chambers - **Circulatory System**: Developed closed circulatory system like annelids/chordates - **Evolutionary Apex**: Most intelligent invertebrates - **Modern Examples**: Nautilus, octopus, squid, cuttlefish ##### Scaphopus → Scaphopods - **Lazy Lifestyle**: Lived underground - **Tusk Shells**: Elongated conical shells - **Brain Reduction**: Simple, brainless creatures - **Foraminifer Predators**: Fed on microscopic protists - **Limited Success**: Small, specialized group ## Biological Accuracy ### End-Botomian Extinction - **Real Event**: First major Cambrian extinction (~513 mya) - **Archaeocyath Extinction**: Major reef-builders went extinct - **Trilobite Decline**: Significant reduction in diversity - **Cause**: Likely combination of climate change, volcanism, anoxia ### Mollusk Phylogeny - **Wiwaxia**: Real Cambrian organism, possible mollusk ancestor - **Shell Evolution**: Accurate progression from multi-plate to specialized forms - **Major Classes**: Accurately represents polyplacophorans, bivalves, gastropods, cephalopods, scaphopods, monoplacophorans ### Anatomical Features - **Chiton Plates**: Eight articulated shell plates - **Bivalve Hinge**: Ligament and muscle system for opening/closing - **Gastropod Torsion**: 180Â° twisting of body during development - **Cephalopod Intelligence**: Largest brains among invertebrates - **Dual-life capability** - survive when waters receded - **Drought survival** by breathing air from sky - **Gift of dual breath** protected through drought and flood #### Tetram - The Revolutionary Breather - **Linear gut** transformation for eating giant fish - **Revolutionary breathing** through **otic notches** (ears) instead of nostrils - **Transcendent power** but **weakened hearing** as trade-off ## The Great Terrestrial Lineage ### The Succession to Land - **Kenicthus** → **Tetracan** and **Rhizodon** - **Tetracan** → **Tetramegas** and **Canowin** - **Eotetras** → **Tintetra** and **Tristichos** - **Platelpis** → **Elpis** (wanderer) and **Platycephalus** (strong skull) ### The Great Love Story - **Pandericthus** searched for perfect love - **Found Stega fair** - marriage blessed - **Son Tictalicus** - destined landwalker supreme ### The Royal Lineage - **Tictalicus** → **Elgin** → **Ventas** → **Acanthos** → **Icthyos** ### Icthyos: The Breathing Revolution - **Stopped breathing through ears** (painful) - **Connected nostrils to mouth** for cleaner airflow - **Perfect sensory ability** - clear hearing and smelling ### The Watcher: Complete Terrestrial Life - **Built no gills at all** - lived wholly on land - **First full terrestrial** vertebrate lifestyle - **Two sons**: **Crassigar** (returned to sea) and **Tetrus** (father of land nations) ## Major Themes - **Progressive terrestrial adaptation** - **Innovation costs and trade-offs** - **Choice between aquatic and terrestrial life** - **Love and partnership driving evolution** - **Complete transition from sea to land** ## Biological Connections - **Rhipidistians** - lobe-finned fish ancestral to tetrapods - **Lungfish** - air-breathing drought survivors - **Otic notches** - early tetrapod breathing structures - **Choanae** - internal nostrils - **Tiktaalik/Acanthostega** - transitional forms - **Tetrapod evolution** - fish to amphibian transition Rhipidistius survives catastrophe; Dipnos breathes both air and water as lungfish; Tetram innovates ear-breathing; Tiktaalik walks the land; Ichthyostega corrects the ear-breathing flaw, restoring smell and sound.

**Pioneer of respiratory art** ### Pulmon's Three Sons - **Siphonogloss** - **Oceanus** - heart of seafaring tradition - **Terron** - spread across land where rivers meet sea ## The Ocean Dynasty ### Oceanus' Maritime Empire - **Roamed vast ocean expanse**, waves and currents as guide - **Saltwater ran deep** in all he did ### Oceanus' Two Sons #### Siphonar - The Bridge Breather - **Chose liminal domain** where sea meets rocky shore - **Air-breathing limpet** without shame - **Clung to rocks** where waves and breezes meet - **Gills transformed** to breathe atmosphere - **Kept ocean's rhythm** while embracing air #### Sacos - The Solar Pioneer - **Unusual path** - ate algae, made shell like glass - **Absorbed solar power's golden wrath** - **Shell became window** to capture light rays - **Sunbeams danced in belly** converting light to food - **"No longer shall I breathe air - sun shall be my energy"** - **Photosynthetic lifestyle** - revolutionary energy source ## Major Evolutionary Innovations ### Respiratory Revolution - **Air breathing** in gastropods - **Gill to lung** transformation - **Liminal breathing** (sea-air interface) - **Beyond breathing** - solar energy adoption ### Energy Strategies - **Traditional air breathing** (Pulmon, Siphonar) - **Photosynthetic energy** (Sacos) - **Hybrid approaches** (maintaining ocean connection) ### Habitat Adaptations - **Open ocean** (Oceanus) - **Intertidal zone** (Siphonar) - **Solar-dependent** lifestyle (Sacos) - **Terrestrial expansion** (Terron) ## Biological Connections - **Pulmonata** - air-breathing gastropods - **Siphonariidae** - air-breathing limpets of intertidal zones - **Solar-powered sea slugs** (Elysia) - photosynthetic gastropods - **Gastropod terrestrialization** - snail and slug land colonization ## Major Themes - **Energy source diversification** - from food to sunlight - **Habitat bridge-building** - connecting marine and terrestrial - **Revolutionary lifestyle** - abandoning traditional breathing - **Innovation through specialization** - **Multiple solutions** to terrestrial challenges The chapter shows the final stages of gastropod terrestrialization and the revolutionary adoption of photosynthetic energy sources, representing one of the most innovative solutions to terrestrial life challenges.

chapter_summaries.1: Aster, a catgirl, spins the universe from a ball of yarn and makes Andromeda as her companion and lover, but the two drift apart, and the yarn Aster throws between them snaps into the Triangulum and Magellanic galaxies until their union at the Omega Point.
chapter_summaries.2: Aster shoots a red thread and Andromeda a blue one across space, but neither reaches the other until Triangulum and the Magellanic Clouds tie the strings together with green, and the listener is told that every life is a thread in their reunion.
chapter_summaries.3: Bound to Andromeda by Lambda, Aster stirs her milk into the Milky Way and makes a family of star sisters: Juno of rogue planets, Brunhilda of failed stars, Ruby the red dwarf, Chrystella of the main sequence, Celestella of supergiants, and Gigastella, whose collapse leaves a black hole.
chapter_summaries.4: Rhodes, son of Ruby, and Marigold, of Chrystella's line, become the first lovers among the stars; as Marigold ages into a white dwarf, their love bursts out in recurring novas that make lithium, remembered today in ruby, topaz and opal wedding rings.
chapter_summaries.5: Aster makes her milk pregnant with cat seed, filling the galaxy with hydrocarbons, planets and oceans where life begins on every world, while Andromeda watches from afar with pride.
chapter_summaries.6: Aster's essence falls as tholins onto the shores of Hesper under the sun Tezca, and in the sea it begins to make itself and multiply, starting the line of life that leads from microbes to humankind.
chapter_summaries.7: Alarmed by how fragile life is on Hesper, Aster weaves phospholipid shells for her creatures, and the brothers Bios, Viros and Dedos trace their line through Benzette, Hesper and Quinamette and name Aster their Greatest Grandmother.
chapter_summaries.8: Bios spreads life by dividing, Viros by viral replication, and Dedos rejects the protective shell until his line dies of starvation and radiation; then a meteor strikes Hesper and the survivors are flung to Phaestia, a moon of the gas giant Venti.
chapter_summaries.9: On Phaestia, under the sun Ehēca, the people honor Aster by many names, among them Suiten, Myoken, Konjin-sama, Brahma, Vairocana and Varuna, until volcanic eruptions tear the moon apart and fling its cyborgs out among the stars.
chapter_summaries.10: The cyborgs settle Serenitide, a moon under the star Quiyah, and build a golden age of cities and temples to Aster and Andromeda; when the moon freezes they move beneath the ice, until a meteor shatters it and casts them toward a fourth sun.
chapter_summaries.11: Under the sun Attle the children settle Kolob, where the Anti-Alpha, born of love denied, turns the people against Aster and against each other, and the Berserkers rain comets on the divided world until the survivors are flung toward Sol.
chapter_summaries.12: On Pluto, Nolah of the line of Bios and Nemla of the line of Viros recite their ancestors through Hesper, Phaestia, Serenitide and Kolob, vow to keep the cosmic yarn unbroken, and hear Aster promise that their roots will grow deep in this system.
chapter_summaries.13: The Sun's nebula forms its planets: Mercury loses its water, Venus is struck into a backward spin, Earth becomes Gaia, Mars dries out, Ceres stays small, and Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune gather their moons, out to the icy Oort Cloud.
chapter_summaries.14: The daughters of Nolah and Nemla leave Pluto for Titan and its five seas, then Enceladus, Saturn's rings, Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto and Mars; they watch Earth shattered by an impact, survive the war of fire and frost on Venus, and settle on the Moon.
chapter_summaries.15: Finding the Moon too dry, the daughters accept the moon goddess Usagi Luna's promise of an elixir of immortality and settle Earth on Vaalbara, building a zircon shrine at Jack Hills, where Luca hears Luna vow that her children will one day be freed from time.
chapter_summaries.16: Luna foretells to Luca that her daughters Arka and Bacta will divide the Earth; temples rise at Isua, Acasta, Jack Hills and Barberton, and Arka's line spreads through Dipana, Yuri with Methana, Halo and Pyra, and Proteus, whose Asgarda bears Heimdalla, Odina, Thora, Lokia and Hela.
chapter_summaries.17: Bacta's daughters Hydra and Terra found the bacterial clans: Hydra's line runs through Proteus, Aqua, Alif, Rachel, Kalia, Splauron and Chloram, while Terra's children Actano and Fermus give rise to Saya, who drinks the sun and releases oxygen, Chloroflexa, Firmicutie and Conan.
chapter_summaries.18: In a peaceful age of the daughters of Arka and Bacta, Saya's greed for yield floods the air with oxygen; the Elohim, Sol, Gaia and Luna plead for restraint, but Rara's lies undo the pacts made at Kamo and Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and a Fimbulwinter freezes the Earth.
chapter_summaries.19: During the Fimbulwinter the viral Gravros and the archaean Mardöll begin the line that produces Euka, the first eukaryote, who casts out the grasping Lilith, mother of parasites, and weds her sister Eve under Mithra's blessing; their children Reticulus, Golgi, Flagella and the rest build the cell.
chapter_summaries.20: Euka lists the gifts of his organelle children, and his line passes through Seth, Resan, Theron and Protea to the twins Chronos, grandfather of the euglenids, and Bios-Neos, father of Nectarius, whose children Plantus, Opima, Cortica and Animus arise as Snowball Earth thaws.
chapter_summaries.21: Under Mithra's blessing Nectarius weds Ambrosia, who bears Animus, Plantus, Opima and Cortica; Plantus takes in Chlora to gain the chloroplast, his heir Plastidus fathers the glaucophytes, red algae and green plants, and Ozymandias, heir of Animus and Opima, fathers Podius and the loveless Metamon.
chapter_summaries.22: Glauca keeps to cloning while Alga weds Alges and bears Rhodes of the red algae and Vert of the green; Ochros steals Rosa to found the diatoms and kelp, Alveolus takes Okra and fathers the ciliates and the parasitic line of Myzo, and Rhizar, Oomy and Haptos band together to win sunlight.
chapter_summaries.23: Hilluhengweh strikes Earth with a gamma ray burst that wipes out most red algae, leaving Lifthasir and Embla, whose inbred descendants turn green; in the aftermath Rhizar's descendants spread, Paulinellus weds a cyanobacterium, and the line of Testatus, Radios, Gromius and Foramer builds shelled kingdoms.
chapter_summaries.24: Choanos and Chana begin multicellular life; their descendants double their colonies each generation, Eudorinus weds Zoe Xanthella to begin farming, Sexagesmus's shieldmaidens drive off invading bacteria and become the mesoderm, and Volvox-Choan's split into Germlings and Somatics provokes Carcinoma's revolt.
chapter_summaries.25: Carcinoma, her genome broken by gamma rays, defies Mithra, makes herself immortal and leads the somatic cells in a Bacchanalia that turns the city into Gehenna, while the faithful Anima and Metazo flee to found the Animal Kingdom, guarding the genome with telomere limits.
chapter_summaries.26: Metazo and Anima's son Therion fathers Porifer, the first sponge, whose line runs through Wallas and Solenos; Vitrius kills his father Leucon and rules from a glass house until his brother Spongius shatters it with a stone, and Demos and Aristos found the living sponge lines.
chapter_summaries.27: Anu's son Enki builds a galley of countless oars and, lost at sea, takes on the Flamens, whom the gods Tyrosine, Tryptophanes, Glutama, Mithra, Iodina and Kali arm with neurotransmitters, giving rise to stinging cells and nerves; his son Xiangus founds the comb jellies while Paraxus takes another path.
chapter_summaries.28: Hecate gives Paraxus the Hox genes and bilateral symmetry; his sons are Cnider, Placus and Bilateron, who gains eyes and with Vendia fathers Xenus and Coelomus, whose line through Nephrus and Cambrius develops the anus, the body cavity, kidneys and the segmented body.
chapter_summaries.29: Beside Lichen Lake the fungal lord Symbio-Mygus weds the alga Charina-Planta and fathers the lichens of every form; the fungus Glomer builds the Wood Wide Web to feed his sister Ashley's land plants, and the spread of these partnerships brings on the Cryogenian ice age.
chapter_summaries.30: Cnider, bound by a pact with Luna to spawn at the full moon, fathers Anthus, ancestor of anemones and corals, and Anaxydros, whose sons Pompom and Meduson found the stalked and swimming jellyfish, among them the box jellies of the caring father Cubos.
chapter_summaries.31: After Cambrius dies, his sons Protos and Dutrus quarrel over whether the first opening is the mouth or the anus; their sons Dietrich, Saccorhytus, Ectus and Spiralius found rival tribes, and Ectus, turned predator, declares the war that opens the Cambrian explosion.
chapter_summaries.32: Ectus, the first predator, strips his body down for burrowing and hunting; his son Ishmael fathers the priapulids and mud dragons, and Isaac fathers Nematus, ancestor of the roundworms and through Gordy of the hairworms, and Rhineheart, whose son Loricus founds the armored loriciferans.
chapter_summaries.33: The conservative Spiralius fathers Kimberella, a famous king, and Gnathifer, who builds chitin jaws; Gnathifer's line produces the jaw worms, the many-jawed Xenognath, the wheel-fishing rotifers of Rotiferus with the parasite Acanthus, and through Amisquius the arrow worms.
chapter_summaries.34: Of Dutrus's twin sons, Saccorhytus stays a larva while Dietrich grows gill slits, a tail, a heart and nerve cords; Dietrich's twins Ambulus and Chordatus father the echinoderms and acorn worms and, through the notochord, the chordates, as the Ediacaran world ends in the Fortunian age.
chapter_summaries.35: In the Tommotian age the sponge Cyath builds the first reefs, and after Gracilis puts down the would-be star emperor Xenu, the line of Lobopus splits into three houses: Velvetclaw, whose Annika founds the velvet worms; Waterbear, from Ferox and Ursus; and Ironfoot, whose Arthur becomes the first arthropod.
chapter_summaries.36: Arthur Ironfoot's descendants spread: Pantopus and Pyka found the sea spiders, Euthyphro's sons Insectus and Arachnus father the insects, crustaceans and arachnids, Euthy ventures onto the shore, and Trilobeth, of Trilos's line, mothers the trilobites who rule the Yakutian seas.
chapter_summaries.37: Chordatus and Annelidus build hearts and closed blood vessels; Annelon's sons Ribbon and Segmentus found the ribbon worms and segmented worms, whose descendants include fire worms, peanut worms, bobbit worms, feather dusters, the vent farmer Hestia, and Clitella, mother of earthworms and leeches.
chapter_summaries.38: Ambulus's son Hemichus founds the hemichordates through Acorn and Oak, and Oak's line passes through the armored Biscarpon, the lopsided Soluton, the three-armed Helicoplacus and the five-sided Pentus to Echidna, mother of the echinoderms and their sea lily cities.
chapter_summaries.39: As Hengweh and Mithra battle in the sky and the first mass extinction kills reef builders and trilobites, Mithra chooses Wiwaxius to restore life; his son Molluscus fathers Testar, whose descendants found the chitons, bivalves, snails, cephalopods and tusk shells.
chapter_summaries.40: Amaterasu's light feeds a sea of plankton: cyanobacteria preyed on by viruses, Roseobella, the choanoflagellates, cannibal dinoflagellates cleared away by rotifers, Xanthus sheltering in the radiolarian Acanther, Sargassos and the fungi of Chytros, and Chordatus's descendants Lancelot and the tunicates, among them Larvaceus, the sea squirts and Salpus.
chapter_summaries.41: Vertebratus builds a bony spine, Rene gathers the organs into the body's core, Hemos gains a large brain and red blood cells from Hausa, the little fish Haikus learns to swim free by believing he can, and Denton invents enamel teeth, honored with tooth-brushing rites, before ghosts end the Cambrian.
chapter_summaries.42: After the extinction the dragon Leviathan, son of the wicked king Magog, rules in peace, and his son Ordovices sets the corals, coralline algae and bryozoans to building reef cities, bringing the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, the first golden age of life.
chapter_summaries.43: While trilobites rule the seas, Crustaceus finds no free home yet founds a line: Mushi's descendants become the copepods, brine shrimp and water fleas, and Karkon's the seed shrimp, tongue worms, barnacles, whose Goose is said to father geese, and through Malacus the crabs, shrimp and isopods.
chapter_summaries.44: Gastropus twists his sons so they can withdraw into their shells; the steadfast Limpus, who teaches building on rock, fathers the limpets, while Snellon's line gives rise to turban snails, abalones, cowries, cone snails, conches, nudibranchs, sea butterflies and Pulmon, the first air-breathing snail.
chapter_summaries.45: Esther, of Echidna's line, bears Blastosa and Crinosa, mothers of the blastoids and crinoids; Crinosa's son Luther breaks his stalk to walk free, his sons Asteros and Echinos go to war, and Ophis and Britta marry across the feud to found the brittle stars, beside starfish, urchins, sand dollars and sea cucumbers.
chapter_summaries.46: The bivalves rise against the old brachiopods: Bivos's children Aphrodite and Peter found the oysters, scallops and river mussels, Clammon's sons the cockles, giant clams, shipworms, geoducks and Venus clams, while Brachios's conservative houses of Lingulus and Articulus hold on as an unknown threat approaches.
chapter_summaries.47: The cephalopods rise: Cameromagne of the line of Endos overthrows the sons of Leviathan and his son Endoceras grows twenty cubits long, while through Actinos come Tarphy, ancestor of the nautilus, Ascos, who breaks off his shell for grace, and tiny, countless Bacchus.
chapter_summaries.48: The land plants of Stomatos spread, draw carbon from the air and chill the Earth; King Hirnan dikes the land, the trilobites die storming it, his sons Moses and Osiris father the mosses, hornworts and ferns, and phosphorus runoff poisons the seas, ending the Ordovician golden age.
chapter_summaries.49: Fleeing Anomalocaris, Euthy leaps onto land to save her eggs; her daughter Myry, given breathing holes, founds the myriapods, her son Cain murders Abel and they father the centipedes and millipedes, the fungi Hera and Freyr wait to bear the higher fungi, and Stomatos takes pores to found the land plants.
chapter_summaries.50: From the ruins of the Ordovician, Silur, son of Chelicer, takes the crown; his son Chasmas's line produces horseshoe crabs, harvestmen through the motherly Opiliona, mites, sun spiders, book scorpions and Ricinus, father of the blood-drinking ticks that carry Lilith's diseases.
chapter_summaries.51: Eurypter and Pulmona's sons Eurypteron and Styloner divide the world between them; Eurypteron's line produces the great clawed Pterygo and Scorpio, who walks onto land as the first scorpion, while Styloner's line takes the rivers through Hibbert and Mycterops, whose son Minirachne climbs ashore to challenge Scorpio.
chapter_summaries.52: Vater, called Abraham, joins liver and pancreas through his ampulla; his son Hestracon builds the stomach, and their descendants keep inventing: Thelos breaks armor into scales, Cephalus gains a lateral line, Osteos makes living bone, and Beakon, Gnathus and Pelaca turn gill arches into the first jaws.
chapter_summaries.53: Polycomb, a sporophyte held in her mother's womb, burns the PRC2 scripture that binds her, grows stomata and rhizoids and, blessed with auxin by Tryptophanes, turns toward the light; her daughter Knoxy and Xylon build xylem, their son Pholon builds phloem, and Tracheus founds the vascular plants.
chapter_summaries.54: In Devon's age of gilled, jawed fish, his descendants branch out: Antiarchon leads guerrilla antiarchs, Mary of Ptycho's line first bears live young, Arthur the Younger founds the arthrodires whose Brachy line produces the giant Dunkella, and Maxil's line through Janusicthus leads to the bony fish.
chapter_summaries.55: The clever but unwise Neo fathers Ammon and Coleos, the ammonites and coleoids; the line of Malacus divides into amphipods, isopods and decapods, from which come prawns, shrimp, lobsters, mud shrimp, squat lobsters and the hermit crab Paguros, as the Protean revolt against Devon fails.
chapter_summaries.56: Arboreus, son of Tracheus, divides the world between Lycos, ancestor of club mosses, spikemosses and quillworts, and Ginkgon, whose leafy line through Phyllon produces Pteridos, father of horsetails and ferns, and Gymnos, while the swamps prepare for Osticthus's sons to come ashore.
chapter_summaries.57: Janusicthus's sons pray for relief from poisoned waters; the Elohim give Chondricthus a keen nose and Osticthus eyes that see color; Acanthus builds a cartilage skeleton, Osticthus learns to gulp air in the river Elivagar, and his sons Sacropter and Actinus found the lobe-finned and ray-finned fish.
chapter_summaries.58: Dikar, a two-nucleus fungus of Freyr and Hera's line, fathers Ascus and Baston, whose descendants include the fission yeasts, Melchizedek of bread and beer, the cup fungi, lichens, Penicillius, the rusts, the corn smut Ustella, the jelly fungi, and Agaricus, father of the mushrooms.
chapter_summaries.59: Mithra sends the prophets Shesha and Matsya to warn of coming doom; the land creatures listen but the sea mocks them, and the Kellwasser and Hangenberg events destroy the reefs, armored fish and most trilobites and sea scorpions, until Mithra tells Matsya each age must remember the last.
chapter_summaries.60: After Romer's gap, Rhea bears Romulus and Remus; Romulus blinds Remus, whose line lives in dark aquifers, and Romulus's son Hexapus founds the six-legged line, whose descendants glide on gill-wings until Hexapter flies and Insectus fathers the mayflies, dragonflies and the folding-winged insects.
chapter_summaries.61: Rhipidistius survives the extinction and fathers Dipnos, ancestor of the lungfish, and Tetram, who breathes through his ears; Tetram's line runs through Pandericthus and Stega to Tictalicus, then to Icthyos, who breathes through his nose, and the gill-less Watcher, whose son Tetrus fathers the land vertebrates.
chapter_summaries.62: Pulmon, a son of Gastropus, learns to breathe air, and his heirs spread the pulmonate snails through sea, shore, river and mountain: Siphonar the air-breathing limpet, Sacos who feeds on sunlight through a glassy shell like the sacoglossan sea slugs, and Acox who returns to the water.
chapter_summaries.63: Amphibos, son of Tetrus, keeps one foot in the water and fathers the amphibians of the coal swamps: Temna of the temnospondyls with Eryops and Mastod, Rana of the frogs, Salamandrus of the salamanders and the cave-dwelling Proteid, and Caecila of the blind, burrowing caecilians.
chapter_summaries.64: Amnios, elder son of Tetrus, invents the amniotic egg with its four membranes, freeing his young from water, and fathers Synaps and Sauros; Synaps's synapsid line runs through sail-backed Pelyon, the pelycosaurs and Dimetrodon, toward Theraps and the whiskered, burrowing Cynos.
chapter_summaries.65: Sauros, second son of Amnios, opens windows in his skull and fathers the reptiles: Paraps and the Turtlos line of turtles, and Eureps, whose sons Squamos (lizards, snakes, tuatara) and Archon (crocodilians, pterosaurs and dinosaurs to come) descend from the coal-swamp Hylonomus.
chapter_summaries.66: Neopter, who folds his wings, fathers the insect orders: Blattus of the cockroaches and termites, Orthopteros of grasshoppers and crickets, Hemipteros of the true bugs, Coleopteros of the countless beetles, Diptos of the flies, and later Hymenos of ants, bees and wasps and Lepidopteron of butterflies.
chapter_summaries.67: Minirachne brings silk-spinning spinnerets onto land, and his son Arachnus becomes father of the spiders: Mygalos of the burrowing trapdoor spiders and tarantulas, and Araneo, whose sideways fangs and orb webs fill the Carboniferous coal-swamp forests.
chapter_summaries.68: Actinus, son of Osticthus, stays in the water with a swim bladder and fathers the ray-finned fishes: Bichiros of the bichirs, Chondrosteos of sturgeons and paddlefish, Holosteos of gars and bowfins, and the vast Teleosteos, whose protruding jaws carry the teleosts into every water.
chapter_summaries.69: Gymnos, son of Phyllon, makes the naked seed and moves from the coal swamps to dry uplands, fathering the gymnosperms: towering Cordaios of the cordaites, slow Cycados of the cycads, needle-leaved Conifera of the conifers, and Ginkga of the long-enduring ginkgo.
chapter_summaries.70: The shelled cephalopods split in two: Ammonos fills the seas with ornate ammonites until all die at the end of the Mesozoic, while Coleios turns his shell inward and fathers the coleoids, Belemno of the belemnites, Sepos of the cuttlefish, Teuthis of the squid and Octopos of the octopus.
chapter_summaries.71: Malacos gives his sons stalked eyes and nineteen-segment bodies, fathering the malacostracan crustaceans: Decapos of lobsters, crabs and shrimp, Euphausios of the krill that feed the whales, Stomatos of the mantis shrimp, and Isops of the pill bugs that walk onto land.
chapter_summaries.72: Acanthus, son of Chondricthus, keeps a cartilage skeleton and fathers Chimaera of the deep-sea ratfish and Elasmos, whose sons Selachios (the sharks, among them Carboniferous Stethacanthos and freshwater Xenacanthos) and Batos (rays and skates) hunt with endless teeth and electric sense.
chapter_summaries.73: As Pangea closes and the Carboniferous coal swamps dry out, Lycos and his lycopsid trees retreat to the coasts and become coal, while Gymnos sends his children Conifera, Ginkga and Cycados to claim the dry highlands, river valleys and desert margins.
chapter_summaries.74: In the Permian, Theraps rises from Synaps's line to succeed sail-backed Pelyon and Dimetrodon, pulling his legs under his body so he can run and breathe at once, growing teeth of different kinds, and fathering the therapsids, among them the heavy-headed dinocephalians.
chapter_summaries.75: Sauros's two children take different roads through the dry Permian: Paraps the parareptile armors himself like the pareiasaurs and passes that armor to Turtlos the turtle, while Eureps opens windows in his skull, leading toward lizards, snakes, archosaurs and birds.
chapter_summaries.76: The continents join into Pangea, whose dry interior swings between heat and cold; small creatures thrive there, as Neopter's insects (beetles, proto-termites, early hymenopterans) spread across the supercontinent and Arachnus's spiders follow them with their webs.
chapter_summaries.77: Cynos the cynodont grows incisors, canines and grinding cheek teeth, jaw bones that begin moving toward the ear, and whiskers that mean hair and warm blood; he digs burrows and warms his young, habits that will save his line in the coming extinction.
chapter_summaries.78: Gorgo the gorgonopsid, saber-toothed apex predator of the late Permian, hunts the herds of Dicyno's dicynodonts across the Pangean plains, picking out the weak, while predator and prey shape each other in a balance that will soon end.
chapter_summaries.79: Before the end-Permian extinction, the Permian sea is shown at its fullest: rugose corals building reefs, Coleios's squid, octopus, belemnites and cuttlefish, coiled ammonites, and Malacos's lobsters, krill and mantis shrimp, all soon to be struck down.
chapter_summaries.80: Dicyno the dicynodont, beaked and tusked, digs roots and crops tough plants across Pangea, becoming the most abundant large land animal of the late Permian in hundreds of species, from rabbit-sized to hippo-sized, and the food that sustains Gorgo's gorgonopsids.
chapter_summaries.81: On the last evening of the Permian, Dicyno's herds graze, Gorgo watches from her ridge, Cynos digs his burrow and the seas are full, while beneath Siberia magma builds and the first sulfur gas escapes unnoticed.
chapter_summaries.82: The Siberian Traps erupt for a hundred thousand years, and acid rain, ocean acidification and anoxia bring the end-Permian extinction, killing 96 percent of marine species, the last trilobites and rugose corals, Dicyno's starving herds and Gorgo's gorgonopsids.
chapter_summaries.83: After the end-Permian extinction, fungi spread over the dead world and rebuild its soil, while the burrowing Cynos and the dicynodont Lystro, Lystrosaurus, survive and have the empty early Triassic land almost to themselves.
chapter_summaries.84: Life returns in the early Triassic: mosses colonize bare rock, Conifera's dormant seeds sprout, the surviving cynodonts of Cynos's line spread into empty niches toward the first mammals, and Teleosteos's teleost fishes begin to fill the healing sea.
chapter_summaries.85: In the Triassic, reptiles return to the sea along the road first taken by the Permian Mesos, Mesosaurus: Ichthyos and giant Shonisauros of the ichthyosaurs, the snub-nosed Thalattos of the thalattosaurs, long-necked Nothros of the nothosaurs, and shell-crushing Plakos of the placodonts.
chapter_summaries.86: Archon, youngest son of Eureps, founds the archosaurs with a four-chambered heart; his elder son Cruros's crocodile-line rauisuchians and phytosaurs rule the Triassic lowlands, while the small, hollow-boned Avemeta, ancestor of the dinosaurs, keeps to the dry uplands.
chapter_summaries.87: Tanystros, Tanystropheus, a Triassic archosauromorph with a neck three times the length of his body, fishes from the Tethys shore without swimming, while his long-necked protorosaur kin wade and paddle at the sea's edge before dying out before the Jurassic.
chapter_summaries.88: Avemeta's first dinosaurs, Deinos and his kin, live small and two-legged in the Gondwanan uplands with Eoraptoros and Herrerasauros while Cruros rules the lowlands; from Deinos branch Theros of the theropods, Sauropos of the sauropods and Ornithis of the bird-hipped ornithischians.
chapter_summaries.89: Ichthyos's ichthyosaurs lose their legs and take the dolphin shape, with flippers, fluked tail, dorsal fin and huge eyes, giving live birth at sea; giant Shonisauros grows as long as a whale, the same form that sharks, tuna and dolphins reach by convergence.
chapter_summaries.90: The sauropterygians of Sauropteros, Nothros the nothosaur and Plakos the placodont, are traced back to Paraps as marine kin of Turtlos the turtle; Nothros's flipper-swimming descendants move to the open sea and become Plesios, the plesiosaurs.
chapter_summaries.91: Pangaea begins to rift into Laurasia and Gondwana with the Tethys Sea widening between them, and the Carnian Pluvial Episode floods the dry Triassic world with rain, weakening Cruros's crocodile-line archosaurs and giving Deinos's dinosaurs a foothold.
chapter_summaries.92: Under the archosaurs, the children of Cynos shrink and take to the night, and in the late Triassic the smallest of them become Mammos, the first true mammals, with three middle-ear bones, milk and fur, beginning a hundred-million-year vigil.
chapter_summaries.93: Coelos, Coelophysis, a slender late Triassic theropod, hunts in coordinated packs through the dry uplands of Gondwana, taking small ornithischians, rhynchosaurs and prosauropods, as a mass grave at Ghost Ranch later shows.
chapter_summaries.94: Pteros, from a branch near Avemeta's root, stretches his fourth finger into a membrane wing and becomes the first vertebrate with powered flight: the small, toothed, insect-eating Triassic pterosaurs, whose line will later include giant Quetzal.
chapter_summaries.95: At the end of the Triassic the recovered world is full again, but the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province begins to erupt along Pangaea's rift; Cruros's phytosaurs and rauisuchians begin to fail, while his small crocodile ancestors and Deinos's dinosaurs hold on.
chapter_summaries.96: The CAMP flood basalts bring the end-Triassic extinction, ending Cruros's rauisuchians, phytosaurs and aetosaurs; Deinos's dinosaurs spread into the emptied lowlands, while Ichthyos, the descendants of Nothros and the small crocodile ancestors survive into the Jurassic.
chapter_summaries.97: In the early Jurassic, Conifera's forests return and Deinos's children take the empty lowlands: Theros's theropods claim the predator's place, Sauropos's sauropods grow long necks to reach the canopy, and Ornithis's ornithischians graze the undergrowth.
chapter_summaries.98: Nothros's heirs become Plesios, the plesiosaurs of the open Jurassic and Cretaceous seas: long-necked Elasmosauros and the big-headed pliosaurs of Plios, both swimming on four flippers like their sea turtle kin and bearing live young.
chapter_summaries.99: Cruros's crocodilian heirs go to sea in the Jurassic as Thalattosuchus, the thalattosuchians: the fully marine metriorhynchids of the Metrion clan, with flippers and tail flukes, and the gharial-like coastal teleosaurids, a line that dies out before the Cretaceous.
chapter_summaries.100: In the middle Jurassic, Sauropos's sauropods grow into the largest land animals: tall Brachio, Brachiosaurus, whip-tailed Diplodos, Diplodocus, and later Argentinosauros, breathing through air-filled bones, kept warm by their own bulk, and moving in herds.
chapter_summaries.101: Feathers first grow on small theropods for warmth, then for display, and in the late Jurassic lagoons of Solnhofen Archaeos, Archaeopteryx, a toothed, clawed, long-tailed theropod with flight feathers, begins the line of the birds.
chapter_summaries.102: In the Jurassic, Theros's theropods fill every predator niche: hatchet-skulled Allos, Allosaurus, hunts sauropods with slashing bites, alongside horned Ceratosauros, the megalosaurids, early spinosaurids and chicken-sized compsognathids, in an arms race with Sauropos.
chapter_summaries.103: In the early Cretaceous, Angios, daughter of Gymnos, brings the flowering plants, which trade nectar for pollination and fruit for seed dispersal; Neopter's insects diversify with them, and hadrosaurs, ceratopsians and night-foraging mammals come to depend on them.
chapter_summaries.104: In the late Cretaceous, Mosas, a monitor-lizard child of Squamos, takes to the sea as the mosasaurs, growing to seventeen meters with flexible, snake-like jaws and a flattened tail, and takes the place of Ichthyos's ichthyosaurs, which die out in the mid-Cretaceous.
chapter_summaries.105: Tyrannos, Tyrannosaurus, the late Cretaceous culmination of Theros's theropods, is twelve meters long, with tiny arms, depth-perceiving eyes, a keen nose and the strongest bite of any land animal, crushing the bones of his prey.
chapter_summaries.106: Ornithis's herbivores answer the tyrant: Ceratops and his horned, frilled kin Triceratops, Styracosauros and Centrosauros defend their herds, Hadros's duck-billed hadrosaurs such as Parasauros call through hollow crests, and armored Ankylos swings a bony tail club.
chapter_summaries.107: In the late Cretaceous, Pteros's pterosaurs reach their greatest size: Quetzal, Quetzalcoatlus, an azhdarchid as tall as a giraffe with an eleven-meter wingspan, soars and stalks the plains, while ornithocheirids and crested pteranodontids fish over the seas.
chapter_summaries.108: The late Cretaceous greenhouse world is at its fullest: Mosas and Plesios in the seas with ammonites and teleosts, Tyrannos, Ceratops and Hadros on land, early birds and Pteros's azhdarchids in the air, flowers and insects everywhere, and Mammos's small mammals in the undergrowth.
chapter_summaries.109: A ten-kilometer asteroid, nudged by Jupiter, falls toward Earth while Tyrannos hunts, Ceratops grazes, Hadros calls and Mammos shelters in his burrow, and it strikes the shallow sea at Chicxulub with the energy of ten billion Hiroshimas.
chapter_summaries.110: The last day of the Cretaceous passes like any other: Tyrannos hunts Ceratops, Hadros herds migrate along the coast, Mosas surfaces in the inland sea, Plesios hunts the deep, Mammos watches the sunset, and at night the asteroid's light grows in the sky.
chapter_summaries.111: The asteroid strikes Chicxulub, and earthquake, tsunami, a burning sky and impact winter collapse the food web, killing Tyrannos, Ceratops, Hadros, the last sauropods, Mosas, Plesios, Pteros's pterosaurs and the ammonites: three quarters of all species die in the end-Cretaceous extinction.
chapter_summaries.112: The small survive the end-Cretaceous extinction: Mammos the mammal in his burrow, the seed-eating birds that are the last dinosaurs, Cruros's crocodiles and Turtlos the turtle; the mammals then spread into the empty Paleocene world, the start of the road toward minds.
chapter_summaries.113: After the impact winter, four lineages walk into the Paleocene: Turtlos the turtle, Cruros's crocodilians, Neornis the crown birds fed on dormant seeds, and Mammos the mammal, who for the first time finds a daylight world free of dinosaurs.
chapter_summaries.114: Neornis's crown birds spread into the niches the dinosaurs left: Gastornis the giant flightless predator of the Paleocene, Passeros's songbirds with their two-voiced syrinx, Aquilos's eagles, hawks and falcons, and the penguins, albatrosses, pelicans and flamingos of the waters.
chapter_summaries.115: Monotremos, eldest branch of Mammos's house, keeps the egg and nurses through milk patches without nipples; carried to Australia from a once-forested Antarctica, his line survives as Ornithorhyncos the electro-sensing platypus and Echidos the spiny echidna.
chapter_summaries.116: Marsupios, second branch of Mammos's house, bears tiny young that grow in a pouch; isolated in Australia her line becomes Macropos the hopping kangaroo, Thylacos the wolf-like thylacine and giant Diprotodontos, while in the Americas only the opossum Didelphis spreads north.
chapter_summaries.117: Placentos, youngest branch of Mammos's house, develops the placenta and the long gestation that allows larger brains, and divides by continent into Afrotheros in Africa, Xenarthros in South America (sloths, armadillos, anteaters, glyptodonts) and Boreos in the north, parent of Euarchos and Laurasios.
chapter_summaries.118: In isolated Africa, Afrotheros's children prove to be cousins: Proboscidos the elephant, whose matriarchs carry the herd's memory and call in infrasound, Hyracos the small rock hyrax, Sirenios the manatees and dugongs, and Oryctos the solitary aardvark.
chapter_summaries.119: In the northern lands joined by Beringia, Boreos divides into Euarchos, ancestor of primates and rodents, and Laurasios, whose children include Chiropteros the echolocating bat, hunter of the night sky, and the hoofed ungulates that run on the Miocene grasslands.
chapter_summaries.120: Carnos, the carnivorans of Laurasios's line, divides into Felidos the ambushing cat and Canidos the pack-hunting dog, with Smilodos the saber-tooth stabbing Pleistocene megafauna, Pinnipedos the seals, sea lions and walruses, and fierce mustelids such as otters and honey badgers.
chapter_summaries.121: When Gramineos, the grasses, spread in the Miocene, Artiodactylos's even-toed hoofed animals take the open plains with running hooves, high-crowned teeth and the fermenting ruminant stomach: Cervidos the deer with yearly antlers and Bovidos the cattle, sheep, antelopes and goats.
chapter_summaries.122: Mammals return to the sea three times: whales evolve from wolf-sized Pakicetos through Ambulocetos, Rodhocetos and Basilosauros into Odontocetos the echolocating toothed whales and Mysticetos the baleen whales, including the blue whale and singing humpback, alongside Pinnipedos's seals and Sirenios's sea cows.
chapter_summaries.123: Rodens the gnawer, with ever-growing self-sharpening incisors and fast breeding, becomes the most numerous order of mammals, while the beaver Castoros builds dams and meadows, the squirrel Sciuros plants oaks from forgotten caches, and the rat Rattus follows humans into their cities.
chapter_summaries.124: In the Paleocene forests Primos gains forward-facing eyes, grasping hands and a growing brain; Lemuros is carried away on Madagascar, Tarsios hunts by night with huge eyes, and Aegyptopithos of Egypt's Fayum Depression appears as the first higher primate.
chapter_summaries.125: In the Oligocene, monkeys raft from Africa across the Atlantic to South America and become the broad-nosed Platyrrhinos with prehensile tails; the howler Alouattos holds territory by voice, the capuchin Cebos uses tools, and the marmoset Callithrinos raises its young cooperatively.
chapter_summaries.126: Catarrhinos splits into tailed monkeys and apes; Cercopithecos thrives in Africa and Asia, the baboon Papios descends to the savanna in hierarchical troops anchored by female lines, the macaque Macacos spreads from Japan to North Africa, and the leaf-eating Colobos ferments leaves in a chambered stomach.
chapter_summaries.127: In the Miocene the apes lose the tail and learn to swing arm over arm; Proconsulos is the first ape, the gibbon Hylobatos sings duets, the orangutan Pongos maps fruit trees in Borneo and Sumatra, and Dryopithos in Africa leads toward the tool-using great apes.
chapter_summaries.128: As late Miocene Africa dries and the Rift Valley opens the savanna, the chimpanzee Panos stays in the forest with learned tool cultures and cooperative hunts at Taï and Gombe, while Sahelanthropos and Ardipithos begin walking upright toward the grassland.
chapter_summaries.129: In the Pliocene Rift Valley, Australos walks fully upright, makes Oldowan stone tools, scavenges wildfire and shares food in bands, while Homo habilis enlarges the brain and helpless infants begin the long human childhood of learning.
chapter_summaries.130: Adam is one ordinary African man of about two hundred thousand years ago from whom every living man inherits his Y chromosome; his root line, Haplogroup A, stays in Africa among the San and Mbuti, and the deeper A00 of the Perry case hints at archaic admixture.
chapter_summaries.131: The first Y-chromosome splits are cast as Adam's sons: Cain the tiller kills the shepherd Abel and his own line dies out, Abel's line becomes Haplogroup B and stays in Africa, and Seth becomes BT, whose descendants through Enosh to Lamech will leave Africa.
chapter_summaries.132: Ten generations after Seth, Noah's people reach the Red Sea as drought and rising seas close in, and Noah builds a small boat and carries his sons Shem, Ham and Japheth across the Bab al-Mandab to Yemen, bringing Haplogroup CT, ancestor of all non-African men, out of Africa.
chapter_summaries.133: Along the coast of Asia, CT splits into DE and CF, and Haplogroup D spreads across southern Asia until the Toba eruption in Sumatra nearly destroys it, leaving survivors only in Japan, Tibet and the Andaman Islands, which share the lineage but no common culture.
chapter_summaries.134: CF splits into C and F, and Haplogroup C appears in two distant peoples: the Aboriginal Australians, with fifty thousand years of unbroken life on their continent, and the Mongols, Kazakhs and other steppe nomads, kin by one lineage that never split into separate names.
chapter_summaries.135: From F's branching through IJK and IJ comes Haplogroup I, the hunter-gatherers who settle Europe, likely paint Lascaux and Chauvet, outlast the ice age in Iberia, Italy and the Balkans, and survive today in Scandinavia, the Balkans and Sardinia beneath later farmer and steppe layers.
chapter_summaries.136: Haplogroup G builds Göbekli Tepe, where the Gaiad holds that the temple led to farming, then carries wheat and herds from the Fertile Crescent into Anatolia and Europe; Ötzi and Sardinian shepherds carry G, and Melchizedek is read as the last priest of Göbekli Tepe's order.
chapter_summaries.137: Haplogroup J stays in the Near East and splits into J1, the Arabian desert line of the Bedouin, and J2, the Levantine and Anatolian line that joins G in founding Sumerian and Akkadian cities like Uruk, Ur and Eridu, where writing and Gilgamesh begin and from which Abraham will come.
chapter_summaries.138: Haplogroups H, L and T share the Indus Valley civilization of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, a planned Bronze Age culture whose script cannot be read, which fades as the Saraswati dries before R1a-carrying Aryans arrive, and whose people survive in modern South Asians.
chapter_summaries.139: Haplogroup N goes north into Siberia and the boreal forest, and its Uralic-speaking descendants, the Finns, Estonians, Sami, Samoyeds and the Magyars who carry their language to Hungary, keep their old speech and the Kalevala's Väinämöinen against the later Indo-European tide.
chapter_summaries.140: Haplogroup O settles the river valleys of China and invents rice farming at Hemudu and Liangzhu, spreading it to Southeast Asia, Korea and the Yayoi of Japan, carrying five language families, the unbroken Chinese script from the Shang, and the Austronesian voyagers who reach Hawaii and New Zealand.
chapter_summaries.141: At Lake Baikal in Siberia, Haplogroup P, called Paikal, forks into Q, which crosses Beringia to people the Americas, and R, which turns back west toward the steppe, a fork recorded in the Mal'ta boy buried near Irkutsk twenty-four thousand years ago.
chapter_summaries.142: R returns west to the Pontic-Caspian steppe, and its sons R1a and R1b are read as Manu and Yemo, the Indo-European twins of the first sacrifice; the horse-riding Yamnaya spread Indo-European languages across Europe, India and the Tarim Basin and overrun Cucuteni-Trypillia.
chapter_summaries.143: Haplogroup E, alone among the lines that left, returns from the Levant to Africa across a Green Sahara, pushes A and B to the margins, and becomes the line of Egypt's pharaohs, the Berbers, the Horn of Africa and the Bantu expansion, ending the haplogroup chapters.
chapter_summaries.144: On Malta, from about 3600 BCE, a nameless farming people raise the world's oldest freestanding temples at Ġgantija, Ħaġar Qim, Mnajdra and Tarxien and carve the Fat Lady figures, until about 2500 BCE the exhausted island fails and the builders vanish.
chapter_summaries.145: After Menes or Narmer unites the Two Lands of Egypt, Imhotep builds Djoser's Step Pyramid, Sneferu perfects the true pyramid, and Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure raise the pyramids and Sphinx at Giza with paid crews, until the 4.2-kiloyear drought ends the Old Kingdom.
chapter_summaries.146: Sargon of Akkad, a foundling who becomes king, conquers Sumer's city-states and builds the first empire; his daughter Enheduanna becomes the first named author, his grandson Naram-Sin declares himself a god, and drought and the Gutians bring the empire down.
chapter_summaries.147: Stonehenge rises on Salisbury Plain from about 3000 BCE, its bluestones dragged from Wales and its sarsen trilithons aligned to the solstices, and the incoming Beaker people, who replace most of the Neolithic builders, finish the monument instead of destroying it.
chapter_summaries.148: On Crete the Minoans build unwalled palaces at Knossos and Phaistos, with frescoes, plumbing, bull-leaping and a mother goddess served by priestesses, writing in the unread Linear A, until the Thera eruption weakens them and the Mycenaean Greeks take over.
chapter_summaries.149: The Yamnaya ride west into Cucuteni-Trypillia, a peaceful goddess-worshipping culture of huge, periodically burned settlements, replace its men while absorbing its women, and spread Corded Ware and Beaker peoples and Indo-European languages to the Atlantic, a gain the Gaiad counts alongside its cost.
chapter_summaries.150: Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor, is the legendary founder of China on the Yellow River, credited with the cart, silk through his wife Leizu, and medicine, who defeats Chiyou at Zhuolu after Fuxi, Nüwa and Shennong, and is still honored by the Chinese state.
chapter_summaries.151: Ur-Nammu founds the Third Dynasty of Ur, writes the oldest law code and builds the Great Ziggurat; Abraham, son of the idol-maker Terah, flees when Elam sacks Ur, and at Sanliurfa near Göbekli Tepe receives Melchizedek's blessing before going on to Canaan.
chapter_summaries.152: The Amorite king Hammurabi unites Mesopotamia under Babylon and issues his code of 282 laws on a diorite stele showing him before the sun-god Shamash; the Gaiad makes him Abraham's cousin, and after his death the Hittites sack Babylon and the Kassites take power.
chapter_summaries.153: Mentuhotep II of Thebes reunites Egypt, and the Twelfth Dynasty of Amenemhat and Senusret rules from Itjtawy in a classical age of literature such as the Tale of Sinuhe, while the afterlife of Osiris opens to all Egyptians and Canaanites settle the eastern Delta.
chapter_summaries.154: In the Hyksos era, Jacob's son Joseph, sold into Egypt, rises to vizier under a Canaanite pharaoh at Avaris and settles his family in Goshen, where the aged Jacob blesses his twelve sons before dying and being buried at Hebron.
chapter_summaries.155: Around 1500 BCE, R1a-carrying Indo-Aryans cross the Hindu Kush into a declining Indus world and mix with its peoples rather than conquering them, producing the Rig Veda's gods Dyaus, Indra and Agni, the four varnas, Sanskrit, and Rudra, who becomes Shiva.
chapter_summaries.156: Ahmose I expels the Hyksos and the New Kingdom becomes an empire: Hatshepsut trades with Punt, Thutmose III wins at Megiddo, Akhenaten imposes the Aten and, in the Gaiad's reading, persecutes the Israelites, and Ramesses II fights at Kadesh and makes peace with the Hittites.
chapter_summaries.157: The Hittites, an early Indo-European people of Anatolia ruling from Hattusa, sack Babylon under Mursili I, fight Ramesses II at Kadesh, sign the first known peace treaty, honor a thousand gods under milder laws, and fall in the Bronze Age Collapse until their archives are rediscovered.
chapter_summaries.158: The Mycenaean Greeks build walled citadels at Mycenae, Tiryns and Pylos, keep Linear B records later deciphered by Michael Ventris, take over Minoan Crete, fight a real war at Troy, and fall in the Bronze Age Collapse, remembered only in the oral poetry Homer inherits.
chapter_summaries.159: Rama, exiled prince of Ayodhya, loses his wife Sita to the demon-king Ravana of Lanka and wins her back with Hanuman's monkey army across a bridge of stones, and the Gaiad reads his war as an eastern reflex of the Trojan War and a shared Bronze Age story.
chapter_summaries.160: Around 1200 BCE drought, earthquakes, revolt and the Sea Peoples bring down Hattusa, Ugarit, Mycenae and Troy, while Ramesses III saves Egypt, Moses' Israelites appear in Canaan and the Philistines settle the coast, a collapse the Gaiad reads as clearing the way for the Axial Age.
chapter_summaries.161: The last Shang king Di Xin, ruled by the fox spirit Daji, loses the Battle of Muye to King Wu, son of King Wen and advised by Jiang Ziya, and the Duke of Zhou frames the Mandate of Heaven that legitimizes the eight-century Zhou Dynasty.
chapter_summaries.162: From the Cameroon and Nigeria borderland, E1b1a-carrying Bantu farmers with yams, iron and later bananas spread east to the Great Lakes and south to the Cape over two and a half millennia, outgrowing the Khoisan, Pygmy and Nilotic peoples, who survive on the margins.
chapter_summaries.163: Zarathustra, a priest of the Iranian plateau rejected by his people, wins King Vishtaspa to his faith in Ahura Mazda against Angra Mainyu, teaching moral choice, final judgment and the sacred fire, ideas the Achaemenid kings and the Jews returning under Cyrus carry west.
chapter_summaries.164: David, shepherd son of Jesse, kills Goliath, flees Saul, mourns Saul and Jonathan, takes Jerusalem and brings in the Ark, then sins with Bathsheba, is rebuked by Nathan, loses his son Absalom to rebellion, and leaves the throne and the messianic line to Solomon.
chapter_summaries.165: After the Dark Age, Greece rises as rival city-states: Sparta under Lycurgus's laws breeds warriors, Athens moves from Solon to Cleisthenes' democracy, Thales, Pythagoras, Heraclitus and Parmenides found philosophy, Herodotus and Thucydides found history, and the Greeks defeat Persia at Marathon, Salamis and Plataea.
chapter_summaries.166: The Neo-Assyrian kings rule the Near East by terror, deport the ten tribes of Israel and besiege Hezekiah's Jerusalem, until Nineveh falls to the Medes and Babylonians; Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilds Babylon, destroys Solomon's Temple and exiles Judah, and Cyrus takes Babylon.
chapter_summaries.167: In the Babylonian exile, Judean henotheism becomes the claim that Yahweh is the only god, shaped by Ezekiel, Jeremiah and Second Isaiah, Persian ideas, scripture and the synagogue; Ezra, Nehemiah and Zerubbabel lead the return and the Second Temple rises under Persian rule.
chapter_summaries.168: Cyrus the Great of Anshan conquers the Medes, Croesus's Lydia and Babylon and frees exiled peoples to go home; Cambyses takes Egypt, Darius organizes satrapies, the Royal Road and Persepolis and records himself at Behistun, and Xerxes fails in Greece, as Persia rules by tolerance.
chapter_summaries.169: In China's Spring and Autumn disorder, Confucius of Lu fails to find a ruler but teaches ren, filial piety and the cultivated junzi through his Analects, while the legendary Laozi leaves the Dao De Jing at a mountain pass, and Chinese culture holds both together.
chapter_summaries.170: Siddhartha Gautama, a Shakya prince of Lumbini, leaves his palace after the Four Sights, rejects luxury and extreme asceticism, and awakens under the fig tree at Bodh Gaya as the Buddha, teaching the Four Noble Truths and no-self to all castes until his death at Kushinagar.
chapter_summaries.171: In Vyasa's Mahabharata the five Pandava brothers and their shared wife Draupadi lose their kingdom to Duryodhana's loaded dice, return from exile, and win the war at Kurukshetra after Krishna teaches Arjuna the Bhagavad Gita, before Yudhishthira's last walk into the Himalayas.
chapter_summaries.172: After the Persian Wars, Athens turns the Delian League into an empire and under Pericles builds the Parthenon, stages Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and Aristophanes, and hears Socrates, executed in 399 BCE, whose students Plato and Aristotle follow, until the Peloponnesian War ends its golden age.
chapter_summaries.173: In fourth-century Greece, Plato's Academy teaches the Forms and the philosopher-king, Aristotle of Stagira tutors Alexander and founds the Lyceum, Diogenes, Pyrrho and Epicurus found the Cynic, Skeptic and Epicurean schools, and Philip II's victory at Chaeronea ends the free city-states.
chapter_summaries.174: Alexander of Macedon inherits Philip II's army, razes Thebes, beats Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela, takes Tyre and Egypt, founds Alexandria, burns Persepolis, defeats Porus at the Hydaspes until his men refuse to go on, and dies at thirty-two in Babylon.
chapter_summaries.175: Chandragupta Maurya, guided by Chanakya's Arthashastra, overthrows the Nandas and defeats Seleucus to found India's first great empire at Pataliputra; his grandson Ashoka, horrified by the Kalinga War, turns to Buddhism, carves his Dhamma edicts on pillars and sends missionaries across Asia.
chapter_summaries.176: Qin Shi Huang conquers the Warring States, unifies China's script, weights and roads, links the Great Wall, burns books and is buried with the Terracotta Army; his dynasty falls within years, and Liu Bang's Han Dynasty rules four centuries, opening the Silk Road under Emperor Wu.
chapter_summaries.177: Rome, a republic that has taken Italy, fights Phoenician Carthage three times: it wins Sicily at sea, survives Hannibal's crossing of the Alps and his victory at Cannae until Scipio Africanus beats him at Zama, and finally razes Carthage as Cato demanded.
chapter_summaries.178: The Gracchi die for land reform, Marius and Sulla turn the legions into private armies, Caesar crosses the Rubicon and is murdered by Brutus, Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra at Actium to become Augustus, and the Pax Romana runs through Titus's sack of Jerusalem to Marcus Aurelius.
chapter_summaries.179: Returned exiles rebuild the Temple as Ezra reads the Torah and Nehemiah raises the walls; Antiochus IV defiles the Temple, Judas Maccabeus retakes it, Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and Zealots divide Judea, Pompey and Herod the Great come, and John the Baptist preaches at the Jordan.
chapter_summaries.180: Jesus of Nazareth, baptized by John, preaches the kingdom of God in Galilee through parables, the Beatitudes and love of enemies, heals and calls twelve disciples, is betrayed by Judas, crucified under Pilate at Golgotha, and is proclaimed risen from the tomb.
chapter_summaries.181: Emperor Ming of Han dreams of a golden man and brings Buddhism to China at the White Horse Temple, Princess Heo Hwang-ok of Ayodhya sails to marry King Suro of Gaya in Korea, and under Kanishka's Kushans Gandhara carves the first Buddha images as Mahayana spreads along the Silk Road.
chapter_summaries.182: Elagabalus, the teenage Severan emperor and hereditary priest of Emesa's sun god, brings the god's black stone to Rome, provokes scandal with his marriages and wish to be a woman, and is killed by the Praetorian Guard, while Aurelian later makes Sol Invictus Rome's god.
chapter_summaries.183: After Elagabalus, Rome suffers fifty years of short-lived emperors, plague and debased coinage; Decius persecutes Christians, Shapur I captures Valerian, Aurelian defeats Zenobia of Palmyra and enthrones Sol Invictus, Diocletian forms the Tetrarchy, and Constantine wins at the Milvian Bridge.
chapter_summaries.184: Ardashir I overthrows the Parthians in 224 and founds the Sassanid Empire at Ctesiphon with Zoroastrianism as state religion; Shapur I captures Valerian, Mani preaches, Khosrow I rules a golden age, and after Khosrow II's war with Heraclius the last shah, Yazdegerd III, is murdered at Merv.
chapter_summaries.185: Armenia, tracing itself to Hayk, becomes the first Christian state when Gregory the Illuminator converts King Tiridates III in 301; Mesrop Mashtots creates the Armenian alphabet, and Vardan Mamikonian dies at Avarayr in 451 resisting Sassanid demands to return to Zoroastrianism.
chapter_summaries.186: In the highland Kingdom of Aksum, King Ezana converts to Christianity through Frumentius around 330; the Ethiopian Church joins the Oriental Orthodox, the Kebra Nagast traces the royal line to Solomon and Sheba through Menelik I, Lalibela carves rock churches, and Ethiopia later defeats Italy at Adwa.
chapter_summaries.187: Constantine wins at the Milvian Bridge in 312 under the chi-rho, legalizes Christianity, founds Constantinople and calls the Council of Nicaea; Theodosius outlaws paganism, Alaric sacks Rome in 410, Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus in 476, and Justinian briefly reconquers the West.
chapter_summaries.188: Zhang Jue's Yellow Turban Rebellion of 184 breaks the Han Dynasty, and the warlords Cao Cao, Liu Bei and Sun Quan divide China into Wei, Shu and Wu after 220; through three centuries of division Buddhism takes root through Kumarajiva's translations and Daoism becomes an organized church.
chapter_summaries.189: Luo Guanzhong's novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms retells the Peach Garden Oath of Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, Zhuge Liang's strategy and the Battle of Red Cliffs in 208, through the fall of Shu, Wei and Wu to the Jin, with Guan Yu later worshipped as the god Guandi.
chapter_summaries.190: Japanese tradition traces Emperor Jimmu from Amaterasu and the sea dragon gods to the founding at Kashihara in 660 BCE; Yamato Takeru wields the sword Kusanagi, Empress Jingū invades Korea while carrying Ojin, the kofun mounds rise, and the Soga clan makes Buddhism the state religion in 587.
chapter_summaries.191: Pre-Islamic Arabia holds Qahtani and Adnani tribes, the idol-filled Kaaba of Mecca under the Quraysh, Jewish tribes at Yathrib and Christian monks; in the Year of the Elephant, 570, Abraha's attack on Mecca fails and Muhammad is born, and in 610 Gabriel brings him the first revelation at Hira.
chapter_summaries.192: Muhammad receives the Quran, preaches tawhid in Mecca, makes the Hijra to Medina in 622, fights at Badr, Uhud and the Trench, and takes Mecca; after his death in 632 the caliphs Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali lead the conquests until the Umayyads take power and Sunni and Shia divide.
chapter_summaries.193: The Tang monk Xuanzang travels illegally to India in 629, studies at Nalanda and returns in 645 with 657 Sanskrit texts to translate; nine centuries later Wu Cheng'en's novel Journey to the West sends him with Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing through eighty-one trials.
chapter_summaries.194: The monk Kūkai brings Shingon Buddhism from Chang'an to Japan, founds Mount Kōya and teaches buddhahood in this very body, while his contemporary Saichō founds Tendai on Mount Hiei, source of Japan's later schools; in the new Heian era Shinto kami and Buddhas merge under honji suijaku.
chapter_summaries.195: Charles Martel stops the Umayyads at Tours in 732, Pepin founds the Carolingian line, and Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne emperor in 800; Byzantium endures iconoclasm until 843, Cyril and Methodius give the Slavs a script, the Treaty of Verdun divides the empire, and Viking raids begin at Lindisfarne.
chapter_summaries.196: The Tang Dynasty rises under Taizong, Empress Wu Zetian rules in her own name, and the An Lushan Rebellion of 755 wrecks Xuanzong's reign; in 845 Emperor Wuzong's Huichang Persecution destroys Buddhist temples, leaving Chan and Pure Land to endure until the Tang falls in 907 and the Song reunifies China.
chapter_summaries.197: The Abbasids found Baghdad and its House of Wisdom, where al-Khwarizmi, Ibn Sina, Ibn al-Haytham and others carry Greek and Indian learning forward; Córdoba and the Fatimids rival them, the Bavandid Qarin of Tabaristan converts in 842, the Seljuks win at Manzikert, and the Mongols sack Baghdad in 1258.
chapter_summaries.198: In Heian Japan the Fujiwara regents peak under Michinaga while court women such as Murasaki Shikibu, author of the Tale of Genji, and Sei Shōnagon write in kana; the Taira and Minamoto clans rise, the Genpei War ends at Dan-no-ura in 1185, and Minamoto no Yoritomo founds the Kamakura Shogunate.
chapter_summaries.199: Snorri Sturluson's Eddas preserve the Norse myths of Odin, Thor, Loki, Yggdrasil and Ragnarök, while Viking raiders reach Iceland, Greenland and Vinland, found Kievan Rus, convert under Vladimir and by vote of Iceland's Althing, and through Rollo's Normandy produce William the Conqueror's victory at Hastings in 1066.
chapter_summaries.200: Saint Patrick's Ireland keeps learning alive through Iona and the Book of Kells, Vikings found Dublin and the first towns, and Brian Boru unites the island as High King before dying at Clontarf in 1014; the Normans invade in 1169, while Eriugena and the Táin of Cú Chulainn carry older traditions forward.
chapter_summaries.201: After the Guptas, India divides into regional kingdoms as Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva shape Vedanta, bhakti spreads and Nalanda falls in 1193; the Cholas build Thanjavur, Mahmud of Ghazni raids Somnath, the Delhi Sultanate rises after Tarain, Timur sacks Delhi in 1398, and Vijayanagara lasts until Talikota.
chapter_summaries.202: Pope Urban II launches the First Crusade in 1095, which takes Jerusalem in 1099; Saladin retakes it, Richard the Lionheart fights him to a truce, and the Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople before Acre falls in 1291, while David the Builder wins at Didgori and the Bavandid line reaches Yuri of Moscow through Anna.
chapter_summaries.203: Temujin rises from poverty and captivity to unite the Mongols as Genghis Khan in 1206, then conquers Western Xia, Jin China and the Khwarazmian Empire; after his death in 1227 Ögedei and Batu take Kiev and reach Hungary, and the Pax Mongolica opens the Silk Road to travelers like Marco Polo.
chapter_summaries.204: Kublai Khan defeats the Southern Song at Yamen in 1279 and rules China as the Yuan Dynasty from Khanbaliq, hosting Marco Polo and losing two fleets to Japan's kamikaze; Hulagu sacks Baghdad, the Mamluks win at Ain Jalut, and Zhu Yuanzhang's Red Turbans drive the Mongols out to found the Ming in 1368.
chapter_summaries.205: Hulagu Khan destroys the Assassins of Alamut in 1256 and sacks Baghdad in 1258, killing the last Abbasid caliph, before the Mamluks Qutuz and Baybars defeat Kitbuqa at Ain Jalut in 1260; the Ilkhanate converts to Islam under Ghazan, Rashid al-Din writes a universal history, and the Black Death follows Mongol routes west.
chapter_summaries.206: Batu Khan conquers the Kipchak steppe and sacks Ryazan, Vladimir and Kiev, beginning two centuries of the Tatar Yoke ruled from Sarai, then crushes European armies at Legnica and Mohi in 1241 before Ögedei's death recalls him and spares Vienna.
chapter_summaries.207: Under the Hōjō regents of the Kamakura Shogunate, Hōnen, Shinran, Eisai, Dōgen and Nichiren found new Buddhist schools, and the samurai hold Hakata Bay against Kublai Khan's invasions of 1274 and 1281 until typhoons, the kamikaze, destroy the Mongol fleets, leaving the shogunate exhausted.
chapter_summaries.208: Plague from the steppe reaches Europe when the Golden Horde besieges Kaffa in 1346, kills perhaps a third of Europe by 1351, provokes flagellants and massacres of Jews, strikes Cairo and Yuan China, and leaves labor scarce, the feudal order strained and the Church's authority weakened.
chapter_summaries.209: Emperor Go-Daigo overthrows the Kamakura Shogunate in 1333 and attempts direct rule in the Kenmu Restoration, but Ashikaga Takauji turns on him, founds the Ashikaga Shogunate and splits Japan into Northern and Southern Courts, while the loyal Kusunoki Masashige dies at Minatogawa.
chapter_summaries.210: Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant orphan and former monk, rises through the Red Turban Rebellion, wins at Lake Poyang and founds the Ming Dynasty as the Hongwu Emperor in 1368, ruling through purges; his son, the Yongle Emperor, seizes the throne, moves the capital to Beijing and commissions the Yongle Encyclopedia.
chapter_summaries.211: Timur, a Barlas Turco-Mongol from near Samarkand, sacks Isfahan, Sarai, Delhi and Damascus, captures the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at Ankara in 1402 and dies at Otrar marching on Ming China; his grandson Ulugh Beg builds an observatory, and his descendant Babur later founds the Mughal Empire.
chapter_summaries.212: Lithuania, the last pagan state in Europe, worships Perkūnas, Gabija and Žemyna in sacred groves and grows under Gediminas from the Baltic to the Black Sea until Jogaila marries Queen Jadwiga of Poland and converts in 1386; Poland-Lithuania then defeats the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410.
chapter_summaries.213: Zheng He, a Muslim Hui eunuch serving the Yongle Emperor, leads seven treasure voyages from 1405 to 1433 with giant ships to India, Arabia and East Africa, bringing back a giraffe hailed as a qilin, before Confucian officials end the voyages and China turns away from the sea.
chapter_summaries.214: Johannes Gutenberg of Mainz develops movable metal type, oil-based ink and the printing press in the 1440s and prints the Gutenberg Bible around 1455; by 1500 presses run in over two hundred European cities, spreading science, national languages and Luther's theses, and propaganda as well.
chapter_summaries.215: The Ottoman dynasty grows from Osman I's frontier emirate through Orhan's crossing into Europe, Murad I's victory at Kosovo in 1389 and Bayezid I's defeat by Timur at Ankara, recovers with the Janissaries and great bombards, and under Mehmed II takes Constantinople on May 29, 1453.
chapter_summaries.216: During the Hundred Years' War, Joan of Arc, a peasant girl from Domrémy guided by the voices of saints, breaks the siege of Orléans in 1429 and sees Charles VII crowned at Reims, then is captured at Compiègne and burned at Rouen in 1431, later cleared and canonized.
chapter_summaries.217: As the Ashikaga Shogunate weakens, the Ōnin War of 1467 to 1477 burns Kyoto and opens the Sengoku period, in which retainers overthrow their lords and new daimyō fight for supremacy while the tea ceremony, Noh, ink painting and wabi-sabi flourish, until Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu reunify Japan.
