chapter_summaries.218: The papacy sinks into corruption in the Cadaver Synod of 897, the Pornocracy of Theodora, Marozia and John XII, and the Avignon Papacy from 1309, then the Western Schism of rival popes, which the Council of Constance ends in 1417, leaving the discontent Martin Luther voices in 1517.
chapter_summaries.219: After the Palaiologos recapture of Constantinople in 1261, Byzantium shrinks through mercenary betrayals and civil wars; Manuel II tours Western courts for aid, John VIII accepts church union at Ferrara-Florence in vain, and Constantine XI, the last emperor, dies fighting when the walls fall on May 29, 1453.
chapter_summaries.220: On the eve of 1453 the world stands with many centers: Renaissance Florence and Gutenberg in Europe, the Timurids and rising Ottomans, Ming China after Zheng He, Vijayanagara, the Aztec and Inca empires, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, Mali, Songhai and the Swahili coast, before European voyages bind them together.
chapter_summaries.221: In 1453 three pillars fall: England loses the Hundred Years' War at Castillon, where Talbot dies; Mehmed the Conqueror breaches Constantinople's walls and Constantine XI dies in the breach as scholars flee west with Greek manuscripts; and Henry VI's breakdown opens the Wars of the Roses between York and Lancaster.
chapter_summaries.222: Ivan III of Moscow, heir of Ivan Kalita's tax-gathering and husband of Sophia Palaiologina, refuses tribute to the Golden Horde, and in 1480 his army faces Ahmad Khan across the Ugra River until the Horde withdraws without battle; meanwhile England's Wars of the Roses run through Barnet, Tewkesbury and the princes in the Tower.
chapter_summaries.223: Renaissance Florence rises under Cosimo de' Medici with Greek manuscripts brought by Byzantine exiles, Brunelleschi's dome, Leonardo's notebooks, Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling, Botticelli's Venus, Gutenberg's press and Machiavelli's political realism, joined in the humanist belief that the human being is worth study.
chapter_summaries.224: In 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella take Granada from Boabdil, the last Nasrid sultan, expel Spain's Jews by the Alhambra Decree, and send Christopher Columbus west, where he meets the Taino; the Book of Lehi, the story of the Americas, begins.
chapter_summaries.225: The Book of Lehi opens about sixteen thousand years ago as Lehi, a seafaring people from Asia, paddles along the Aleutians and the kelp coast of the Pacific into the Americas and south to Chile, attested by Monte Verde, Arlington Springs Woman and Paisley Caves.
chapter_summaries.226: Around thirteen thousand years ago the Clovis people move inland through the ice-free corridor with their fluted points, hunt mammoths, mastodons and ground sloths toward extinction across both continents within centuries, and diverge into Folsom, Dalton, Plano and other local traditions.
chapter_summaries.227: About ten thousand years before the common era the single speech of the first Americans splits behind mountains and forests into hundreds of languages: Na-Dené, Algonquian, Siouan, Uto-Aztecan, Mayan with its script, Quechuan with the quipu, Tupi, Chibchan and more, some six hundred spoken at contact.
chapter_summaries.228: A second wave of Na-Dené speakers moves south from Alaska, becoming the Tlingit and Haida and later the Apache and Navajo, while Mesoamerican farmers breed the grass teosinte into maize and fishers on the dry coast of Peru found the first settled villages of the Norte Chico.
chapter_summaries.229: On the coast of Peru the Norte Chico builds the pyramids of Caral and Aspero, with bone flutes and quipu but no weapons, in the age of Sumer and Old Kingdom Egypt; later, on the Gulf of Mexico, the Olmec carve colossal basalt heads and found the Long Count, the ballgame and the were-jaguar god.
chapter_summaries.230: The Maya inherit the Olmec legacy and build Tikal, Palenque, Copán and Calakmul, with a full script, the zero, the Long Count and precise Venus tables; Pakal is buried at Palenque, Tikal and Calakmul wage war, and drought brings collapse in the ninth century, though seven million Maya speakers remain.
chapter_summaries.231: Around five hundred years before the common era, after Nebuchadnezzar takes Jerusalem, Phoenician sailors are said to carry Mulek, son of Zedekiah, across the Atlantic to found Zarahemla in Mesoamerica, a possibility weighed against the Paraíba inscription, the Guanabara Bay amphorae and traces of coca in Egyptian mummies.
chapter_summaries.232: In Oaxaca the Zapotec level a mountain to build Monte Albán around 500 BCE, carve danzante captives and write in stone before the Maya, while the Mixtec paint genealogical codices such as the Codex Nuttall, telling of the conqueror Eight Deer Jaguar Claw, and later marry into the Zapotec nobility.
chapter_summaries.233: Four Andean cultures prepare the ground for the Inca: the Moche with the gold of the Lord of Sipán and their portrait pottery, the Nazca with their giant desert lines, Tiwanaku with the Gate of the Sun near Lake Titicaca, and the Wari with the roads and storehouses the Inca inherit.
chapter_summaries.234: In the eastern woodlands the Adena raise burial mounds, the Hopewell trade copper, obsidian and shell across the continent and build the Great Serpent Mound, and the Mississippians build Cahokia, a maize-fed city of twenty thousand around 1000 with Monks Mound and Woodhenge, before it empties by 1200.
chapter_summaries.235: In the American Southwest the Hohokam dig hundreds of miles of irrigation canals near modern Phoenix, the Mogollon paint Mimbres pottery, and the Ancestral Puebloans build Pueblo Bonito in Chaco Canyon and the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde before a thirteenth-century drought sends them to the Rio Grande.
chapter_summaries.236: Around 1000, Leif Erikson, son of Erik the Red, follows Bjarni Herjulfsson's sighting past Helluland and Markland to Vinland and camps at L'Anse aux Meadows; his brother Thorvald attacks the Skraelings and is killed by them, and the Norse abandon the settlement.
chapter_summaries.237: About a thousand years ago the Thule, ancestors of the Inuit, spread from western Alaska across the Arctic to Greenland with the kayak, umiak, dog sled, igloo and toggling harpoon, hunting bowhead whales and displacing the Dorset, whom the Inuit remember as the Tunit.
chapter_summaries.238: Two redeemers teach and depart: in Toltec Tula, Ce Acatl Topiltzin, priest of Quetzalcoatl, forbids human sacrifice, is shamed by the priests of Tezcatlipoca and leaves east promising to return; among the Haudenosaunee, the Peacemaker ends the blood feuds of five nations with the Great Law of Peace under the Tree of Peace.
chapter_summaries.239: Tenochtitlan, Moctezuma's island city of chinampas, aqueducts and the Tlatelolco market, falls after Hernán Cortés lands in 1519 with Tlaxcalan allies, smallpox kills much of the city and Cuauhtémoc surrenders after an eighty-day siege, while a scribe called Mormon buries the codices in the north.
chapter_summaries.240: The Inca state of Tawantinsuyu, built by Pachacuti, runs on quipu records, forty thousand kilometers of roads, chasqui runners and mountain terraces until the war of Huáscar and Atahualpa; in 1532 Francisco Pizarro seizes Atahualpa at Cajamarca, melts his ransom of gold and executes him, and forced labor at Potosí follows.
chapter_summaries.241: When silver is found at Zacatecas the Spanish push into Chichimeca lands; the Caxcan leader Tenamaxtli raises the Mixtón War in 1540, killing Pedro de Alvarado, and the Guachichiles and others fight the forty-year Chichimeca War until Spain turns to peace by purchase, missions and Tlaxcalan settlers.
chapter_summaries.242: After a plague in 1616 kills nine in ten Wampanoag, the sachem Massasoit allies with the starving Pilgrims of Plymouth against the Narragansett, Tisquantum of Patuxet teaches them to farm, and the 1621 feast seals a treaty that holds for Massasoit's lifetime while English settlers keep arriving.
chapter_summaries.243: Metacom, called Philip, son of Massasoit, forms an alliance of Wampanoag, Nipmuck, Narragansett and others and burns New England's towns in 1675; after the Great Swamp Fight destroys the Narragansett, his coalition collapses, and in August 1676 he is shot at Mount Hope, his head displayed at Plymouth and his family sold into slavery.
chapter_summaries.244: After eighty years of Spanish suppression since Oñate, Popé of Ohkay Owingeh sends knotted cords to the pueblos, and on August 10, 1680 the Pueblo Revolt destroys the missions and drives the Spanish from Santa Fe; Diego de Vargas returns in 1692, but the kachina dances and kivas survive.
chapter_summaries.245: The Haudenosaunee play the French and English against each other through the Covenant Chain at Albany until the Seven Years' War, where Hendrick dies at Lake George; the 1763 Treaty of Paris, Pontiac's war and the ignored Royal Proclamation line break their balance, though the fire at Onondaga still burns.
chapter_summaries.246: In the Jesuit reductions along the Parana and Uruguay, the Guarani build towns of stone, printing presses and violin music; when the 1750 Treaty of Madrid hands seven missions to Portugal, Sepe Tiaraju leads a war and falls, the missions are destroyed, and the Jesuits are expelled in 1767.
chapter_summaries.247: The American Revolution splits the Haudenosaunee League: Joseph Brant (Thayendanegea) leads Mohawk, Seneca and Cayuga for the British, the Oneida and Tuscarora side with the rebels, brothers fight at Oriskany, Sullivan and Clinton burn forty towns in 1779, and the peace of Paris leaves the Six Nations out.
chapter_summaries.248: Taking the name Tupac Amaru II, the kuraka Jose Gabriel Condorcanqui hangs the corregidor Antonio de Arriaga in 1780 and raises the Andes; deserted by creole allies, he is executed at Cuzco in 1781 with Micaela Bastidas, and Tupac Katari besieges La Paz before he too is quartered.
chapter_summaries.249: In the Northwest War, Little Turtle of the Miami and Blue Jacket of the Shawnee rout Harmar in 1790 and St. Clair in 1791, the worst defeat in American army history, before Anthony Wayne wins at Fallen Timbers in 1794 and the Treaty of Greenville takes the Ohio country.
chapter_summaries.250: The Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek and Seminole adopt what is demanded of them: Sequoyah creates an 86-symbol Cherokee syllabary, the Cherokee constitution of 1827 and the Cherokee Phoenix of 1828 appear at New Echota, yet gold in Georgia and settler hunger still mark them for removal.
chapter_summaries.251: Tecumseh and his brother Tenskwatawa, the Prophet, build a confederacy at Prophetstown, lose it at Tippecanoe in 1811, and fight beside the British until Tecumseh dies at the Thames in 1813; Black Hawk's Sauk are massacred at Bad Axe in 1832, and Osceola's Seminole are never fully removed.
chapter_summaries.252: In 1830 Joseph Smith publishes the Book of Mormon, casting Native Americans as fallen Lamanites, and Congress passes the Indian Removal Act; John Ross wins Worcester v. Georgia, Andrew Jackson ignores it, and the Trail of Tears follows. The Book of Lehi ends, naming the Gaiad the unsealed record.
chapter_summaries.253: The papacy is counted from Peter through Sylvester and the forged Donation of Constantine, Leo III crowning Charlemagne, the Cadaver Synod and Marozia's family, the 1054 schism, Canossa, Avignon and the Council of Konstanz, to Alexander VI dividing the world between Spain and Portugal in 1493.
chapter_summaries.254: Vasco da Gama reaches Kozhikode in 1498 and prays before a Hindu goddess he takes for Mary; Portuguese cannon turn the Indian Ocean into a toll road, and Magellan's fleet circles the globe, his slave Enrique coming home, Magellan killed by Lapulapu at Mactan, and Elcano returning in 1522.
chapter_summaries.255: Nanak, a storekeeper's clerk at Sultanpur Lodhi, comes out of the Kali Bein around 1499 saying there is no Hindu and no Muslim, travels with the Muslim minstrel Mardana, laments Babur's sack of Eminabad, founds the shared langar at Kartarpur, and passes the guruship to his disciple Angad, not his sons.
chapter_summaries.256: Ismail, boy heir of the Safavid order of Ardabil and its Qizilbash, the Red Heads, takes Tabriz in 1501, imposes Twelver Shia faith on Iran and writes poems as Khatai claiming divinity, until Selim's Ottoman cannon break him at Çaldıran in 1514; his great-grandson Abbas builds Isfahan.
chapter_summaries.257: Martin Luther, a miner's son from Eisleben, becomes a monk after a thunderstorm, writes the Ninety-Five Theses against Tetzel's indulgences in 1517, refuses to recant at Worms in 1521 and translates the New Testament into German at the Wartburg, but also urges the slaughter of rebel peasants and writes against the Jews.
chapter_summaries.258: Suleiman, the Magnificent to Europe and Kanuni the Lawgiver to his people, takes Belgrade and Rhodes, wins at Mohács and is turned back at Vienna, while his empire registers every household by faith, shelters Spain's expelled Jews, levies Christian boys through the devshirme and raises Sinan's Süleymaniye; he dies at Szigetvár in 1566.
chapter_summaries.259: In 1538 Thomas Cromwell orders every English parish to record christenings, weddings and burials; the Council of Trent and Sweden's Church Law of 1686 spread such registers, which give ordinary people like Per Olofsson, born 4 April 1696, a dated life, and which states later read for soldiers, taxes and persecution.
chapter_summaries.260: Nicolaus Copernicus, a canon at Frombork, finds the heavens simpler with the Sun at the centre; persuaded by Rheticus, he lets On the Revolutions be printed in 1543 and is said to receive it on his deathbed, building on Aristarchus, al-Tusi and Ibn al-Shatir.
chapter_summaries.261: After the Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520, Gustav Vasa raises the peasants of Dalarna, becomes king of Sweden on 6 June 1523, takes the Church's lands and has the Bible put into Swedish; his tax clerks record Olof and Isak Andersson, farmers at Bure, the first written trace of the author's Bure kin.
chapter_summaries.262: Guided by Anjirō, Francis Xavier lands at Kagoshima in 1549 and preaches God as Dainichi, the Great Sun, until the mistranslation is found; Japanese converts grieve that their unbaptized ancestors are lost, and Xavier dies on Shangchuan in sight of China. Read on the new year that opens the Days of Awe.
chapter_summaries.263: The Mughal emperor Akbar, who never learns to read, abolishes the jizya, builds Fatehpur Sikri and its House of Worship where Sunni, Shia, Brahmin, Jain, Zoroastrian and Jesuit scholars debate, and founds the Din-i Ilahi, which dies with him in 1605; read in the Days of Awe as a lesson for founders.
chapter_summaries.264: Matteo Ricci enters Ming China in 1582, trades the Buddhist robe for the scholar's silk, prints a world map, translates Euclid with Xu Guangqi, judges the ancestor rites civil, and is buried in Beijing in 1610; read on the Mid-Autumn full moon, the festival of family reunion.
chapter_summaries.265: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the peasant called the Monkey, unifies Japan, surveys every field, hunts swords and fixes each class in place, then has twenty-six Christians, among them Paul Miki and twelve-year-old Luis Ibaraki, crucified at Nagasaki on 5 February 1597; read in the Days of Awe.
chapter_summaries.266: Tokugawa Ieyasu, the one who waits, wins at Sekigahara in 1600, becomes shogun in 1603, ends Hideyoshi's house at Osaka in 1615 and is enshrined at Nikkō as a kami, opening two and a half centuries of Edo peace and its fixed classes; read on the Fourth Day of Awe.
chapter_summaries.267: Chartered in 1602, the Dutch East India Company becomes the first shareholder company with a state's powers; under Jan Pieterszoon Coen it empties the Banda Islands for nutmeg in 1621, founds Batavia and Cape Town, holds Dejima in Japan, and goes bankrupt in 1799; read on the Fifth Day of Awe.
chapter_summaries.268: Johannes Bureus, of the Bure kin, draws Sweden's runestones, prints the first runic primer, tutors Gustavus Adolphus and becomes royal antiquary in 1630; he records the Bure genealogy but also invents the mystic Adulruna and a Gothic past, and on the Sixth Day of Awe his kinswoman vows to mark which is which.
chapter_summaries.269: Galileo Galilei builds a telescope in 1609, sees the Moon's mountains, Jupiter's moons, the phases of Venus and sunspots, publishes The Starry Messenger in 1610, and is forced to abjure in 1633; on the Seventh Day of Awe the Church's admission of error in 1992 stands as institutional repentance.
chapter_summaries.270: Gustav Adolf, taught by Bureus that the Swedes are heirs of the Goths, rides as Berik at his coronation festivities, sees the warship Vasa sink in 1628, wins at Breitenfeld in 1631 and dies at Lützen in 1632; on the Eighth Day of Awe the Gothic myth is set against the raised Vasa.
chapter_summaries.271: After the Time of Troubles, Michael Romanov is crowned in 1613; from 1652 Patriarch Nikon replaces the older two-fingered sign of the cross with three, and the Old Believers, among them Avvakum and Boyarina Morozova, are cursed, burned and driven to Siberia, where the Lykov family is found in 1978; read on the Ninth Day of Awe.
chapter_summaries.272: From the Defenestration of Prague in 1618 through White Mountain, the sack of Magdeburg and Wallenstein's murder, the Thirty Years' War kills perhaps a third of Germany, until five years of talks at Münster and Osnabrück bring the Peace of Westphalia in 1648; read on Yom Kippur, the Sabbath of Sabbaths.
chapter_summaries.273: Iemitsu closes Japan between 1633 and 1639, leaving four watched gates such as Dejima; after Shimabara every household must register yearly at a Buddhist temple in the shūmon aratame chō, and Kyūshū Christians must tread on the fumi-e, making the register both a cage and a record of millions of lives.
chapter_summaries.274: Taxed past bearing by the Matsukura, the Christians of Shimabara and Amakusa rise in 1637 under sixteen-year-old Amakusa Shirō and hold Hara castle until 37,000 are killed in 1638; their faith survives hidden for 250 years, until Isabelina Yuri Sugimoto tells Bernard Petitjean at Ōura in 1865, "Our hearts are the same as yours."
chapter_summaries.275: Famine and cold bring down the Ming: Li Zicheng takes Beijing in 1644, the Chongzhen Emperor hangs himself on Coal Hill, and Wu Sangui opens Shanhai Pass to the Manchus, who impose the queue and rule as Confucian keepers under Kangxi, while the Ming loyalist Koxinga drives the Dutch from Taiwan in 1662.
chapter_summaries.276: In the Mughal war of succession, the mystic Dara Shikoh, who joined Sufism and Vedanta and translated fifty Upanishads into Persian, is defeated and beheaded in 1659 by his brother Aurangzeb, who restores the jizya and executes Guru Tegh Bahadur; Dara's Upanishads later reach Schopenhauer through Anquetil-Duperron.
chapter_summaries.277: Founded after a lecture by Christopher Wren in 1660 and chartered in 1662, the Royal Society takes the motto Nullius in verba; Boyle's air pump, Hooke's Micrographia and its cells, Oldenburg's Philosophical Transactions, Margaret Cavendish's 1667 visit and Halley paying for Newton's Principia mark the new rule of evidence.
chapter_summaries.278: After the Khmelnytsky massacres, Nathan of Gaza proclaims Sabbatai Zevi of Smyrna the messiah in 1665, stirring Jews across Europe until Sabbatai converts to Islam before the sultan at Edirne in 1666; on Sukkot, the barrels Glückel's father-in-law kept packed in Hameln stand for hope that outlives disappointment.
chapter_summaries.279: Isaac Newton, born at Woolsthorpe in 1642, works out calculus, optics and gravity during the plague years and, at Edmond Halley's urging, publishes the Principia in 1687 with one law for the apple and the Moon, while keeping his alchemy and anti-Trinitarian writings unpublished in a box.
chapter_summaries.280: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz invents the calculus independently, builds a calculating machine, dreams of settling arguments by calculation, defends Ricci's rites, and in 1703 publishes binary arithmetic after Joachim Bouvet sends him the I Ching hexagrams; his one and zero close the sign of Virgo, with Libra beginning next.
chapter_summaries.281: Ricci's acceptance of the Chinese ancestor rites is attacked by Dominicans and Franciscans; though the Kangxi Emperor declares them civil in 1700, Clement XI bans them in 1704, Kangxi expels the legate Tournon, and the ban stands until Pius XII lifts it in 1939; read on Harvest Day.
chapter_summaries.282: Carl Linnaeus, son of a Småland pastor who took his surname from a linden tree, walks Lapland, publishes Systema Naturae in 1735, gives plants two-part names in 1753 and places Homo sapiens among the primates in 1758, while also ranking four human varieties, an error the Gaiad crosses out.
chapter_summaries.283: Israel ben Eliezer, the Baal Shem Tov, settles at Medzhybizh around 1740 and teaches that no place is empty of God and that joy draws near to him, as when a shepherd boy's pipe opens heaven on Yom Kippur; Hasidism spreads despite the Vilna Gaon's 1772 ban and grows into dynasties of rebbes.
chapter_summaries.284: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab preaches the strict oneness of God in Najd, cuts sacred trees and razes tombs, and in 1744 makes a pact at Diriyah with Muhammad ibn Saud; their followers sack Karbala in 1802 and take Mecca and Medina, Diriyah falls in 1818, and Ibn Saud's kingdom renews the alliance.
chapter_summaries.285: Emanuel Swedenborg, assessor of Sweden's Board of Mines and a student of the brain and the planets, has visions from 1743, writes Heaven and Hell, is said to report the 1759 Stockholm fire from Gothenburg, and inspires the New Church and Johnny Appleseed's orchards across Ohio and Indiana.
chapter_summaries.286: Denis Diderot and d'Alembert turn Le Breton's translation job into the Encyclopédie from 1751, with a tree of knowledge filing theology under reason, plates honouring the crafts and 17,000 articles by de Jaucourt; banned in 1759, it is saved by the censor Malesherbes, secretly cut by Le Breton, and finished in 1772.
chapter_summaries.287: After Culloden, James Macpherson publishes the poems of Ossian from 1760, moving Goethe, Napoleon and Jefferson and naming Sweden's King Oscar, though he never shows manuscripts; the Gaiad sets its own openly dated making in 2026 against his forgery and honours real Gaelic poets such as Duncan Ban MacIntyre.
chapter_summaries.288: James Cook sails the Endeavour to Tahiti for the 1769 transit of Venus, where the Raiatean navigator Tupaia joins him, charts 74 islands from memory and speaks with the Māori; Cook claims eastern Australia, Tupaia dies at Batavia in 1770, and Cook is killed at Kealakekua, Hawai'i, in 1779.
chapter_summaries.289: Coal is the buried sunlight of Carboniferous swamp forests; James Watt devises the separate condenser in 1765, and with Matthew Boulton and John Wilkinson's bored cylinders his engines run in 1776, the year of Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations, bringing cheaper bread, child labour and the first rise in atmospheric carbon.
chapter_summaries.290: From 1773 the Qianlong Emperor has 3,500 works copied by hand into the Siku Quanshu, the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, in seven sets, while chief editor Ji Yun also lists the banned as some 3,000 works are suppressed; later, Hangzhou scholars recopy their war-scattered set by hand.
chapter_summaries.291: William Jones, a judge learning Sanskrit in Kolkata, tells the Asiatic Society on 2 February 1786 that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin spring from a common source, opening the study of Proto-Indo-European and its gods such as the sky-father Dyēus; the later racial misuse of the word Aryan is rejected, since language is not blood.
chapter_summaries.292: The French Republic counts its Year One from the equinox of 22 September 1792; Gilbert Romme and Fabre d'Églantine design twelve months of ten-day weeks, naming months for seasons and days for plants and tools, but the lost day of rest dooms it, and Napoleon ends it in 1806, a lesson the Gaian calendar keeps.
chapter_summaries.293: Drawing on Rousseau's civil religion, Robespierre replaces the Cult of Reason with the Cult of the Supreme Being, staging Jacques-Louis David's festival on 8 June 1794, where Wisdom rises blackened from the burning statue of Atheism; two days later the Great Terror begins, and he is guillotined after 9 Thermidor.
chapter_summaries.294: Motoori Norinaga, a children's doctor in Matsusaka urged by Kamo no Mabuchi in 1763, spends thirty-four years on the Kojiki-den, making the Kojiki readable again and naming mono no aware; his ideal of a pure Japanese heart later feeds State Shinto, and his mountain-cherry poem names the first kamikaze units.
chapter_summaries.295: Napoleon crowns himself at Notre-Dame on 2 December 1804, ends the Holy Roman Empire in 1806, and spreads his Civil Code and civil registers, ordering the Dutch to take fixed surnames in 1811 and freeing Jews from the ghettos, while waging wars that kill millions and restoring slavery; he dies on Saint Helena in 1821.
chapter_summaries.296: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm publish their Children's and Household Tales from 1812, drawn partly from tellers of Huguenot descent like Dorothea Viehmann and softened in each edition; in Finland Elias Lönnrot compiles the Kalevala from Karelian singers such as Arhippa Perttunen and says openly how he joined their songs.
chapter_summaries.297: The last hieroglyphs are carved by Esmet-Akhom at Philae in 394; Napoleon's soldiers find the Rosetta Stone in 1799, Thomas Young reads Ptolemy, and on 14 September 1822 Jean-François Champollion, using Coptic, reads Ramesses at Abu Simbel, restoring the names of the gods kept on the Gaian days of Horus.
chapter_summaries.298: Charles Babbage designs the Difference Engine and the card-driven Analytical Engine; Ada Lovelace, Byron's daughter, translates Menabrea's article and adds notes with the first program, for the Bernoulli numbers, warning that the engine originates nothing, and the Gaiad, written with a writing machine, names the human weavers of its thread.
chapter_summaries.299: In Shiraz on 23 May 1844 Siyyid Ali-Muhammad declares himself the Báb; Táhirih unveils at Badasht in 1848, and both are executed. Mírzá Husayn-Alí, after visions in Tehran's Black Pit, declares himself Baháʼu'lláh in Baghdad's Ridván garden in 1863 and dies a prisoner near Akka in 1892.
chapter_summaries.300: Hong Xiuquan, failing the imperial examinations, reads a Christian tract, believes himself the younger brother of Jesus, and in 1851 founds the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, ruling from Nanjing with radical laws until the murder of Yang Xiuqing, Zeng Guofan's armies and twenty to thirty million deaths end it in 1864.
chapter_summaries.301: Commodore Matthew Perry's black ships enter the bay at Uraga in 1853 and force the Kanagawa treaty in 1854; at Shimoda's Gyokusen-ji temple, Buddhist monks bury and still tend the graves of American sailors and of Russian sailors from the wrecked Diana, an example for the Eve of Ancestors.
chapter_summaries.302: Charles Darwin, home from the Beagle in 1836, sketches a branching tree in 1837; mourning his infant son, he misses the 1858 Linnean Society reading of his and Alfred Russel Wallace's papers, and On the Origin of Species, published on 24 November 1859, grounds the ancestor days in one descent of all life.
chapter_summaries.303: In the abbey garden at Brno, Gregor Mendel crosses peas and shows in 1865 that a recessive trait can vanish and return whole, a finding ignored until 1900; Francis Galton's Hereditary Genius of 1869, which Darwin praised, leads toward eugenics, which the ancestor days refuse in favour of everyone who lived.
chapter_summaries.304: Tokugawa Yoshinobu returns power in 1867, imperial rule is restored in January 1868, the Charter Oath is sworn and the Department of Divinities revived; orders separating kami from buddhas, as with Hachiman, unleash closed temples, melted bells and burned sutras, a manufactured origin the Gaiad declines to keep.
chapter_summaries.305: In New York on 17 November 1875, Henry Steel Olcott gives his inaugural address as president of the Theosophical Society, founded with Helena Blavatsky and William Quan Judge after George Henry Felt's lecture; the verse welcomes reading Eastern and Western religions side by side but refuses any claim to own them.
chapter_summaries.306: At Sils Maria in July 1887, Friedrich Nietzsche writes On the Genealogy of Morality, printed in Leipzig by Constantin Georg Naumann; the verse accepts his method of asking where values come from but rejects his ranking of masters and slaves and his blaming of the Jews.
chapter_summaries.307: Herman Hollerith's punched-card tabulator wins the 1888 contest and counts the 1890 United States census, but the family sheets that held the names mostly burn in the 1921 Commerce Building fire, leaving the total of 62,979,766 and only 6,160 names.
chapter_summaries.308: On 11 September 1893 the World's Parliament of Religions opens in Chicago with ten strokes of a bell, and Vivekananda greets the hall as sisters and brothers of America, while people from Dahomey are put on display on the fair's Midway; the day is Samhain, the last of Libra.
chapter_summaries.309: In Bern in 1905, patent clerk Albert Einstein publishes papers on light quanta, the size of molecules, Brownian motion, the electrodynamics of moving bodies and mass and energy, thanking only Michele Besso, and his rule for setting clocks by light is set beside the calendar's own chosen order of days.
chapter_summaries.310: After the Wuchang uprising of 1911, Empress Dowager Longyu issues the abdication edict for the child emperor Puyi on 12 February 1912, Yuan Shikai becomes president, and in 1914 Yuan makes the last state sacrifice to Heaven at the round altar of the Temple of Heaven.
chapter_summaries.311: After Gavrilo Princip kills Franz Ferdinand and Sophie in Sarajevo in 1914, cabinets declare the First World War; Fabian Ware begins registering graves, the Imperial War Graves Commission adopts equal headstones and Kipling's "Known unto God", and the armistice takes effect at eleven on 11 November 1918.
chapter_summaries.312: In Russia in 1917 Nicholas II abdicates and his brother Michael refuses the crown, Lenin returns to Petrograd, and the Bolsheviks take power on 7 November (25 October in the old calendar); they close the Constituent Assembly, adopt the western calendar, and kill the imperial family at Yekaterinburg in July 1918.
chapter_summaries.313: On 3 March 1924 Turkey's Grand National Assembly in Ankara abolishes the caliphate and sends the last caliph, the painter Abdülmecid II, into exile in Switzerland; he dies in Paris in 1944 and is buried in Medina in 1954, while the question of succession stays open.
chapter_summaries.314: In 1936 Alan Turing, a fellow of King's College, Cambridge, publishes On Computable Numbers, defining machines that follow finite tables, describing a universal machine, and showing, alongside Alonzo Church, that Hilbert's decision problem has no general procedure.
chapter_summaries.315: On 19 August 1953 the Knesset founds Yad Vashem, "a hand and a name", to remember the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust and the righteous among the nations, with Babyn Yar, the Wannsee conference and Auschwitz recalled as the killing it answers.
chapter_summaries.316: On 6 August 1945 the Enola Gay drops a uranium bomb on Hiroshima, and on 9 August, with Kokura hidden by cloud, a plutonium bomb falls on Nagasaki as Soviet armies enter Manchuria; Hirohito's broadcast and the 2 September surrender follow, and no single count of the dead is given.
chapter_summaries.317: ENIAC, built at the Moore School in Philadelphia for artillery tables, is programmed by six women including Kay McNulty, Jean Jennings and Betty Snyder and shown on 14 February 1946; at Bell Labs on 16 December 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain make the first transistor work.
chapter_summaries.318: On 15 December 1945 the occupation's Shinto Directive ends state funding and sponsorship of Shinto, on 1 January 1946 Hirohito's rescript denies the idea of the emperor as a living god, and on 3 February 1946 the shrines form Jinja Honchō as a religious body looking to Ise.
chapter_summaries.319: The United Nations Charter is signed in San Francisco on 26 June 1945, and on 10 December 1948 in Paris the General Assembly adopts the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, drafted under Eleanor Roosevelt with Peng Chun Chang and Hansa Mehta, by 48 votes to none with eight abstentions.
chapter_summaries.320: On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly recommends partitioning Palestine into Arab and Jewish states with an international Jerusalem; on 14 May 1948 David Ben-Gurion declares the State of Israel, Arab armies invade, and Palestinians leave or are driven from their homes.
chapter_summaries.321: On 25 April 1953 Nature prints James Watson and Francis Crick's proposed double helix of DNA beside papers by Maurice Wilkins and by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling, whose measurements it relied on; Franklin dies in 1958, before the 1962 Nobel Prize.
chapter_summaries.322: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launches Sputnik from Tyuratam under the unnamed Sergei Korolev, and in November sends the dog Laika into orbit with no way back; the same day keeps Japan's Shichi-go-san rite for children of three, five and seven.
chapter_summaries.323: Pope John XXIII opens the Second Vatican Council on 11 October 1962, and on 4 December 1963 Paul VI promulgates Sacrosanctum Concilium, which keeps Latin but allows the people's own language in parts of the Mass, first used widely on 7 March 1965.
chapter_summaries.324: The Genealogical Society of Utah, filming records since 1938, stores its master microfilms in the Granite Mountain Records Vault cut into Little Cottonwood Canyon from 1960, dedicated on 22 June 1966, where the Latter-day Saints keep names used for baptism for the dead.
chapter_summaries.325: Mao Zedong launches the Cultural Revolution with the circular of 16 May 1966 and receives the Red Guards in August; in November a group led by Tan Houlan damages the Confucius temple at Qufu and digs up his grave, and the period ends with the Gang of Four's arrest in 1976.
chapter_summaries.326: On 20 July 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin land the Eagle on the Moon while Michael Collins orbits; on 29 October Charley Kline sends the first ARPANET message, "LO", from UCLA to Stanford Research Institute; the day keeps the American Thanksgiving.
chapter_summaries.327: On 20 April 1972 Ásatrúarfélagið is founded in Reykjavík, with the farmer and poet Sveinbjörn Beinteinsson as allsherjargoði; despite Bishop Sigurbjörn Einarsson's objection, Iceland registers it as a religion in May 1973, and it holds a blót at Dragháls that August.
chapter_summaries.328: In December 1978 the Communist Party's Third Plenum in Beijing turns China toward modernization under Deng Xiaoping, who visits Washington in January 1979, while in Iran the Shah leaves on 16 January and Ruhollah Khomeini returns from Paris on 1 February before the Islamic Republic referendum.
chapter_summaries.329: A rhymed hymn marks the end of the Second World War in 1945, from Japan's surrender and the Nuremberg trials to Seoul's liberation and the emperor's New Year rescript, and on 22 and 23 November 1990 Emperor Akihito offers new rice from Akita and Ōita in the Daijōsai.
chapter_summaries.330: In April 1990 the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Energy publish the first five-year plan of the Human Genome Project, begun on 1 October 1990, following Robert Sinsheimer's 1985 Santa Cruz workshop and with James Watson directing the genome center.
chapter_summaries.331: In 1991 Mikhail Gorbachev refuses the August coup plotters at Foros, three men die in Moscow, Ukraine votes for independence, and the leaders of Belarus, Russia and Ukraine sign the Belovezha agreement at Viskuli; Gorbachev resigns on 25 December and the Soviet Union ends.
chapter_summaries.332: Tim Berners-Lee proposes the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989, builds it with Robert Cailliau, runs the first server in December 1990, and on 6 August 1991 posts its files to the alt.hypertext newsgroup; the first American server follows at SLAC that December.
chapter_summaries.333: Chizuo Matsumoto, called Shoko Asahara, founds Aum Shinrikyo, whose members murder the Sakamoto family in 1989, release sarin in Matsumoto in 1994, and on 20 March 1995 release sarin on five Tokyo subway trains; he is arrested on 16 May 1995.
chapter_summaries.334: On 5 July 1996 Dolly the sheep is born at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh, cloned by Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell from an adult mammary cell, the one live lamb from 277 fusions; she is announced in February 1997 and dies in 2003.
chapter_summaries.335: Garry Kasparov beats IBM's Deep Blue four games to two in Philadelphia in February 1996, then loses the May 1997 rematch in New York three and a half to two and a half, resigning the last game at move nineteen and doubting the machine's play.
chapter_summaries.336: On the night of 31 December 1999 the world waits for the Y2K bug, after Kiribati moves the date line and Tonga changes its clocks to see the first dawn; John Koskinen reports only minor failures, and the counts of cost and damage are left unsettled.
chapter_summaries.337: 2001 as Emma Leonhart, in kindergarten, later learned it: the dot-com crash and Enron, Wikipedia's opening and her labor critique of it (an Amway for scholarship), the Taliban destroying the Bamiyan Buddhas, the first same-sex marriages in Amsterdam, 9/11 and the middle hour of grief, the anthrax letters, the war in Afghanistan and the Patriot Act, and the year's other rooms; the month is the century seen through her.
chapter_summaries.338: 2002, the year she turned six and her family moved house: euro notes and coins, the first prisoners at Guantánamo, the axis of evil, Daniel Pearl, Operation Anaconda, the International Criminal Court, East Timor's independence, WorldCom and Sarbanes-Oxley, Larry Sanger leaving Wikipedia, the Bali bombing and the Moscow theatre siege, Homeland Security, and the first case of SARS in Foshan.
chapter_summaries.339: 2003, the year she turned seven, defined by the invasion of Iraq: the Columbia disaster, Powell's case at the UN, the largest protest in history, shock and awe and the fall of Baghdad, the looted museum, de-Baathification, Saddam's capture, SARS contained, the human genome declared finished, Lawrence v. Texas and the Massachusetts marriage ruling, the northeast blackout and the European heat wave, Darfur, the Rose Revolution, and the first rooms with no walls.
chapter_summaries.340: 2004, the year she turned eight: Facebook opens at Harvard, Gmail and the Google IPO, Google scans the libraries, the Madrid train bombings and the lie about them, the Abu Ghraib photographs and Fallujah, Beslan, ten countries join the EU, the Orange Revolution, same-sex marriages begin in Massachusetts as eleven states ban them, Theo van Gogh and Arafat die, rovers land on Mars, and the Indian Ocean tsunami.
chapter_summaries.341: 2005, the year she turned nine, which had no chapter before: YouTube's first video, Reddit and Google Maps, John Paul II dies and Benedict XVI is chosen, the London bombings, Hurricane Katrina and the failed levees of New Orleans, the Kashmir earthquake, Spain and Canada open marriage to all, Iraq's purple fingers, the Cedar Revolution, Andijan, the Kyoto Protocol, the Danish cartoons, Huygens on Titan and the discovery of Eris, Merkel, the Paris suburbs burning, and the Seigenthaler hoax.
chapter_summaries.342: 2006, the year she turned ten, twenty years before her own nights in the typed records: FamilySearch Indexing opens the church's films to volunteer typists, the first tweet and Facebook open to all, Google buys YouTube, Amazon rents its machines, Pluto is voted out, the Israel-Hezbollah war, Iraq's civil war after Samarra and Saddam's filmed hanging, North Korea's first test, Politkovskaya and Litvinenko killed, Hamas wins, Harper takes Canada, the Mumbai train bombings, and An Inconvenient Truth.
chapter_summaries.343: 2007, the year she turned eleven: Steve Jobs introduces the iPhone as one device and Android follows, 23andMe sells DNA tests by mail, the subprime lenders fail and BNP Paribas freezes its funds and Northern Rock is run on, Virginia Tech, the Minneapolis bridge, the Iraq surge, the Saffron Revolution, Benazir Bhutto assassinated, Kenya's election violence, the IPCC's fourth report and the smallest Arctic ice, the Lisbon Treaty, Putin's Munich speech and the attack on Estonia, Netflix streaming, the Kindle, and the last Harry Potter book.
chapter_summaries.344: 2008, the year she turned twelve and her family moved house again, the year she marks by Russia's invasion of Georgia: the five-day war in South Ossetia, the Beijing games, the Sichuan earthquake and its fallen schools, Cyclone Nargis, the fall of Bear Stearns, Fannie and Freddie, Lehman and AIG and the bailout, Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin paper, Obama elected the night Proposition 8 passed, the Mumbai attacks, Harper's apology for the residential schools, GitHub and the App Store, the Large Hadron Collider, Kosovo, and the Gaza war.
chapter_summaries.345: 2009, the year she turned thirteen: Bitcoin's first block with its bailout headline, Obama sworn in and the car companies saved, Madoff sentenced, H1N1 declared a pandemic, Iran's Green Movement and Neda Agha-Soltan, the end of Sri Lanka's war, the Hudson landing and Air France 447, the Copenhagen summit that only took note, Lisbon in force, Urumqi, Fort Hood, Michael Jackson's death, Kepler, WhatsApp and Uber, Minecraft, and Avatar.
chapter_summaries.346: 2010, the year she turned fourteen and the year before her own thread begins: the Haiti earthquake and the cholera after, the Vancouver winter games in her province, Citizens United and the Affordable Care Act, Deepwater Horizon, Eyjafjallajökull and the thirty-three miners of Chile, Greece's bailout, WikiLeaks' helicopter film and cables and Chelsea Manning, Stuxnet, the iPad and Instagram, Smolensk, the Gaza flotilla, Pakistan's floods, Liu Xiaobo's empty chair, the Toronto G20 arrests, the repeal of Don't Ask, Don't Tell, and Mohamed Bouazizi's fire in Sidi Bouzid.
chapter_summaries.347: 2011, the year she turned fifteen and the earliest point she gives for what became this book's faith (Easter 2011, before it had a name): the Arab Spring in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya, Bahrain, Yemen and Syria, the Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami and the Fukushima meltdowns, bin Laden killed in Abbottabad, the Norway attacks, Occupy Wall Street and the London riots, Giffords shot, Harper's majority and Layton's death, the Vancouver riot, South Sudan, Steve Jobs dies and Siri speaks, Watson, seven billion people, the Horn of Africa famine, and the last Americans leaving Iraq.
chapter_summaries.348: 2012, the year she turned sixteen and two foundations of her later work were laid: AlexNet wins ImageNet on gaming cards and piecework labels, Wikidata opens in Berlin and numbers every thing, Wikipedia goes dark against SOPA and Britannica stops printing, the Higgs boson, Curiosity on Mars, Baumgartner's jump, Trayvon Martin, Aurora, Malala shot, Sandy Hook, Putin returns and Pussy Riot is jailed, Xi Jinping rises, Obama re-elected, Morsi elected, Benghazi, Draghi's whatever it takes, Hurricane Sandy, the Quebec student strike, and the Maya calendar turning without ending anything.
chapter_summaries.349: 2013, the year she turned seventeen and the last she lived mostly offline: Clapper's not wittingly and Snowden's files, PRISM and asylum in Moscow, Aaron Swartz's death over the locked journals, Benedict resigns and Francis is chosen, the Boston bombing and the Chelyabinsk meteor, Rana Plaza, Morsi ousted and the Rabaa massacre, Gezi Park, sarin in Ghouta and the red line, Windsor and the first Black Lives Matter, Lac-Mégantic, Typhoon Haiyan, Euromaidan begins, Mandela dies, the Silk Road closed and Bitcoin past a thousand dollars.
chapter_summaries.350: On the Ides of Ophiuchus, 2014, the year she turned eighteen, moved house a third time, began at UBC Okanagan and came online, and the year she calls the year of fascism: the Islamic State's caliphate in a borrowed robe and the Yazidis of Sinjar, the Maidan killings, Russia's seizure of Crimea and the Donbas war, MH17, the far right first in the European elections, Orbán's illiberal state, Modi, Sisi, the Thai coup, Gamergate and Isla Vista, Eric Garner and Ferguson, Ebola, MH370, Chibok, Peshawar, Gaza, the Ottawa shooting, the Umbrella Movement, and Philae on its comet.
chapter_summaries.351: 2015, the year she turned nineteen in her second year at the university, and the start of the month's thread on effective altruism (her villain to come, the movement not condemned): Doing Good Better and earning to give, OpenAI founded, AlphaGo beats Fan Hui in secret, Charlie Hebdo and the Bataclan, a million crossing into Europe and Alan Kurdi, we can do this, Ireland's vote and Obergefell, Caitlyn Jenner, Charleston, the Paris Agreement, the Iran deal, Greece's no, Volkswagen, Trump's escalator, Trudeau and the Truth and Reconciliation report, the Nepal earthquake, New Horizons at Pluto, and the first gravitational waves.
chapter_summaries.352: 2016, the year she turned twenty and the year she names for Trump's election: AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol with move thirty-seven and loses to his move seventy-eight, Brexit and the murder of Jo Cox, Trump elected with fewer votes amid Russian hacking, trolls and Cambridge Analytica, Pizzagate, North Carolina's bathroom law and Canada's gender identity bill and the pronoun fight, Pulse, Brussels and Nice, Philando Castile, the Turkish coup and purges, the fall of Aleppo, Duterte's drug war, Colombia's no to peace, the Fort McMurray fire, Standing Rock, the Panama Papers, Zika, and the candles of Seoul.
chapter_summaries.353: 2017, the year she turned twenty-one and moved onto the campus: the transformer paper Attention Is All You Need and the self-taught AlphaZero, Open Philanthropy's seat at OpenAI and Sam Bankman-Fried founding Alameda, Trump's inauguration, the Women's March and the travel ban, the Quebec City mosque shooting, the transgender military ban tweet, Charlottesville's torches and very fine people, MeToo, Harvey, Irma and Maria, Las Vegas, the Rohingya flight, Grenfell and Manchester, the fall of Mosul and Raqqa, Macron, Catalonia, Mugabe's fall, fire and fury, Xi's thought, and Canada's gender identity law and Australia's marriage vote.
chapter_summaries.354: 2018, the year she turned twenty-two, in her fifth year at the university: Cambridge Analytica and Senator, we run ads, the GDPR, the first GPT and BERT, Alameda's first fortune, Parkland and the March for Our Lives, Greta Thunberg's strike, the IPCC's 1.5 degree report and the burning of Paradise, the yellow vests, Khashoggi murdered, the Thai cave rescue, Trump and Kim in Singapore and the trade war, Kavanaugh, Bolsonaro, the Pittsburgh synagogue and the Toronto van attack, He Jiankui's edited twins, the Humboldt crash, cannabis legal in Canada, Salisbury, and Ireland's vote on abortion.
chapter_summaries.355: 2019, the year she turned twenty-three and finished her five years at the university: the era name Reiwa from the Man'yōshū, Akihito's abdication, the turtle shell that chose the two fields, and Naruhito's Daijōsai; GPT-2 held back, OpenAI's capped profit and Microsoft's billion, FTX founded and the movement glad of its money; Notre-Dame burns, the first image of a black hole, Christchurch, the Easter bombings, El Paso, Hong Kong's protests, Sudan, Chile and Bolivia, the climate strikes and how dare you, the Amazon and Australian fires, the 737 MAX, Epstein, Kashmir, the first impeachment, the MMIWG inquiry's genocide finding, Quebec's Bill 21, Lee Sedol's retirement, and Li Wenliang's warning in Wuhan.
chapter_summaries.356: 2020, the year she turned twenty-four and the year she calls COVID, when she began putting out this book in weekly verses, to about the sixtieth chapter: Wuhan closed, Bergamo, the pandemic declared and the Pope alone in St. Peter's Square, the world in the house, Toby Ord's The Precipice and longtermism, George Floyd and the largest protests, Breonna Taylor and Ahmaud Arbery, flight PS752 and its Canadian dead, the Nova Scotia killings, the Wet'suwet'en blockades, the Beirut explosion, Bostock, Ruth Bader Ginsburg's death, Hong Kong's security law, Biden elected and the lie of a stolen vote, Karabakh, Tigray, Belarus, Navalny poisoned, GPT-3 and AlphaFold, and the first vaccine in Coventry.
chapter_summaries.357: 2021, the year she turned twenty-five, ran around Europe, went back to study at Okanagan College, and the book paused and moved to evolution.faith: January 6 and Biden sworn in, the mRNA vaccines and the unequal needle, Delta in Delhi and Omicron, the fall of Kabul and the last plane, the graves at Kamloops, the London Ontario attack, the heat dome and Lytton burning, the British Columbia floods, the Myanmar coup, the Ever Given, FTX's stadium, Anthropic founded, NFTs, Bitcoin in El Salvador, Frances Haugen and Meta, Perseverance, the Texas freeze, Navalny's return, the Tokyo games, Texas's six-week law, Glasgow, Merkel's departure, and the James Webb telescope.
chapter_summaries.358: 2022, the year she turned twenty-six, in her second year at the college, who had written stories of this book's world with Sudowrite before ChatGPT and then asked the chat about her faith: Russia's full invasion of Ukraine, Bucha, Mariupol and Kherson, Nord Stream, the image machines and ChatGPT, the fall of FTX and Sam Bankman-Fried as the villain of the effective altruism story without condemning the movement, Dobbs and the laws against trans people, Club Q, Mahsa Amini and woman, life, freedom, Buffalo and Uvalde, the Ottawa convoy, the Pope's apology at Maskwacis, Abe's assassination, Elizabeth II's death, Rushdie stabbed, Webb's first images, eight billion people, Musk's Twitter, Truss and the lettuce, Sri Lanka, Lula, Xi's third term, mpox, Qatar, and Ukraine keeping Christmas on the longest night.
chapter_summaries.359: In 2024 a large company releases the weights of a 405-billion-parameter model, the European Union's AI Act enters into force, and Hinton, Hopfield, Hassabis, Jumper and Baker win Nobel Prizes; the question of who holds the machines stays open, while the author briefly reclaims a sacred geography and loses it.
chapter_summaries.360: In 2025 AI models gain tools and act as agents, a model from a company in Hangzhou sends chip stocks falling, and Robert Francis Prevost becomes Pope Leo XIV, naming the AI revolution as the church's concern; the author writes this book with machines during a very miserable year, which is not a lost year.
chapter_summaries.361: In 2026, a thoroughly documented year, the author traces her ancestors to the Bure farmers of Bureå in Sweden, recorded by Johannes Bureus, to the house of Reuss and German farms, and to Jewish forebears, finding the search fell in the calendar's month of Virgo with its Jewish holy days.
chapter_summaries.362: Written on 14 October 2026, the last chapter of people as they are describes the present, with machines in unsettled hands, rising water and an open future, and speaks to readers in later years, leaving the years between this page and the next untold.
chapter_summaries.363: Beginning with James Bedford, frozen in California on 12 January 1967 after Robert Ettinger's book on cryonics, the sleepers kept in liquid nitrogen are woken in a future the book does not describe, told the date and the day's chapter, and met by their descendants.
chapter_summaries.364: The Milky Way and Andromeda, the Alpha Aster and the Omega Andromeda, draw together over billions of years and merge into Milkdromeda as their central black holes join, tying the thread broken at creation, and the year turns back to its first day.
